days.title: Resource Hierarchy and Organization Policies: Organizations, Folders, Projects, Constraints and Dry Run

concepts.heading: Organization, Folders and Projects
concepts.body: Google Cloud resources sit in a hierarchy. The organization resource is the root, folders are optional grouping nodes, and projects hold the actual resources such as VMs, buckets and databases. Every resource except the organization has exactly one parent. Folders can contain projects and other folders, nested up to 10 levels, so a common layout is one folder per department with dev and prod folders below it, for example organizations/1234, then folders/News, then folders/News-prod, then projects/news-web-prod. Allow policies, deny policies and organization policies attached to a node apply to everything below it, which is why folders are the natural place to delegate: a department head with an admin role on the department folder controls every project in it and nothing outside it. Google recommends folders under one organization rather than several organizations, because separate organizations have no central visibility and every guardrail has to be copied into each one.

concepts.heading: Where an Organization Comes From
concepts.body: There are two ways to get an organization resource. A company that signs up for Google Workspace or Cloud Identity and verifies a DNS domain gets one automatically; the super admin then hands out the Organization Administrator role (roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin). A new Free Trial customer who signs up with a Google email and has no domain gets a standalone organization instead, named after the user plus -org (renameable later). In a standalone organization the Organization Owner role (roles/cloudowner.admin) is managed outside IAM on the Organization details page; owners can invite more owners, who must accept within 30 days, and service accounts can never be owners. Several owners avoid a single point of failure. Remember that Organization Administrator is an access-management role: it grants roles and sees the hierarchy, but it does not include creating folders or projects.

concepts.heading: Creating Folders and Projects
concepts.body: Creating things needs its own roles: Folder Creator (roles/resourcemanager.folderCreator), Folder Admin for full folder control, and Project Creator (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator). A brand-new organization grants Project Creator and Billing Account Creator to the entire domain so nobody is disrupted; tighten that by removing the domain grants and giving Project Creator to a platform group. From the CLI, `gcloud projects create acme-payments-dev --folder=834512776120` places the project in a folder, and `--organization=ORG_ID` places it directly under the organization; use one parent flag only. The project ID is globally unique and permanent: 6 to 30 characters, starting with a lowercase letter, using lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. The display name is separate and can change at any time. Moving a project to another organization keeps its ID, data, direct roles and billing link, but swaps everything it inherits.

concepts.heading: Organization Policy Constraints and Inheritance
concepts.body: IAM decides who can act; Organization Policy decides what configurations are allowed for everyone, project Owners included. A policy sets a constraint on a node, such as `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` with the value group in:eu-locations, which also covers EU regions Google adds later. List constraints are merged with the parent only when the child sets inheritFromParent to true, and then a denied value always wins over an allowed one. A child policy that does not inherit replaces the parent's policy for that subtree. Boolean constraints such as compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation are never merged: a value set on a project decides for that project, so limit who holds Organization Policy Administrator (roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin). New policies are usually not retroactive: existing non-compliant resources keep running and must be found, for example with Cloud Asset Inventory, and fixed by hand. `gcloud org-policies describe CONSTRAINT --project=ID --effective` shows the policy that actually applies.

concepts.heading: Dry Run and the Security Baseline
concepts.body: Before enforcing a policy that might break workloads, create it in dry-run mode. A dry-run policy is evaluated like a real one and writes violations to audit logs, but nothing is denied, so you can watch for a few weeks, fix or exempt the affected teams, and then enforce. Dry run supports custom and managed constraints (for example compute.managed.vmExternalIpAccess) but only a few legacy ones. Separately, organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 start with a security baseline of enforced policies. Three to know: Domain restricted sharing (iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains) rejects IAM grants to identities outside allowed customers, including personal gmail.com accounts; iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation blocks new service account keys; storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess blocks per-object ACLs. When a grant or key creation fails with an error nobody remembers configuring, check the organization policies first with `gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --organization=ORG_ID`.

examPoints: A question about a role holder who can grant access but cannot create folders or projects is testing that Organization Administrator manages IAM only; creation needs Folder Creator, Folder Admin or Project Creator.

A question where a project still gets a value its folder denies, or still blocks a value the folder allows, is testing list-constraint inheritance: with inheritFromParent the values merge and deny wins, without it the child policy replaces the parent's.

A question that asks how to see the impact of a new guardrail without blocking anyone points to dry-run mode, and a question about outsiders rejected in a new organization points to the security baseline's Domain restricted sharing.

quiz.q: The Dev folder has a policy for compute.trustedImageProjects that allows projects/base-images and projects/team-images. A project in the folder sets its own policy for the same constraint that allows only projects/base-images and does not set inheritFromParent. Which image projects can VMs in this project use?
choices: Both image projects, because a project policy can only add allowed values to the list that its folder already allows
Both image projects, because the folder's policy is evaluated first and the project's own policy is then ignored
Only projects/base-images, because a policy that does not inherit replaces the folder's policy for this project
No image projects, because two conflicting list policies at different levels block the constraint until one goes
quiz.explain: Without inheritFromParent the project's policy replaces its parent's, so only the value listed on the project applies. Choice A is tempting because merging does exist, but values are merged only when the child sets inheritFromParent to true.

quiz.q: A team created a project with the ID acme-tst-1 and the display name Acme Test. Their naming standard now requires the ID acme-test-1. What should they do?
choices: Create a new project with the ID acme-test-1 and move the workloads, because a project ID is permanent
Run gcloud projects update with the new ID, because both the project ID and the display name can be edited at any time
Move the project to another folder and back, because a move between parents lets you choose a new project ID
Ask an Organization Administrator to rename it, because only that role can change a project ID inside the organization
quiz.explain: The project ID is permanent; only the display name can change, so the fix is a new project with the right ID. Choice B is tempting because the update command does exist, but it changes the name, not the ID.

days.recap: The organization is the root, folders group and delegate, and projects hold resources with a permanent ID; organization policies restrict configurations for everyone, list constraints merge only when inheriting (deny wins), boolean ones do not merge, new policies are not retroactive, and dry run plus the security baseline shape how guardrails are rolled out.

days.title: Identities and Access: Cloud Identity Users and Groups, Directory Sync, Project Roles, Workforce Identity Federation and Inventory

concepts.heading: Cloud Identity Users and Groups
concepts.body: People who use Google Cloud need an identity, and for a company that usually means a user in Cloud Identity or Google Workspace. Users and Google groups belong to that identity account, not to a project, and you can manage them in the Admin console, in Google Groups, on the Groups page of the Google Cloud console or with gcloud. The best practice is to grant IAM roles to groups and manage people through membership: adding someone to a group gives them every role the group holds on every project. `gcloud identity groups memberships add --group-email=gcp-analysts@example.com --member-email=lee@example.com --expiration=30d` adds a temporary member. Note who can create groups: group permissions come from Workspace or Cloud Identity admin privileges, not IAM. IAM roles such as Organization Viewer only let someone open the Groups page, so a project Owner can see it and still fail to create a group.

concepts.heading: Google Cloud Directory Sync
concepts.body: Companies that keep Microsoft Active Directory or another LDAP directory as the source of truth automate user management instead of creating accounts by hand. Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS), a free Google tool, queries the LDAP directory and creates, updates and deletes users and groups in Cloud Identity through the Directory API. It usually runs on premises as a scheduled task with a dedicated admin account, so HR changes reach Google Cloud on the next run. Provisioning is one way, from the directory to Cloud Identity, and it does not copy passwords. For sign-in, Cloud Identity is set up for SAML single sign-on, delegating authentication to Active Directory (for example through AD FS), so passwords, MFA and lockout rules stay in one place. A user must be provisioned before SSO can succeed. Small teams without a directory simply create users and groups manually.

concepts.heading: Granting a Role on a Project
concepts.body: Access to a project is defined by its allow policy, a list of bindings that each connect principals to one role. `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding sales-prod --member=group:analysts@example.com --role=roles/bigquery.dataViewer` adds one binding and leaves the rest untouched. The member needs a prefix such as user:, group:, serviceAccount: or domain:, and the role needs its full name. `gcloud projects set-iam-policy PROJECT policy.json` is different: it replaces the whole policy with the file, so an incomplete file silently removes other people's access. Roles come in three kinds: basic, predefined and custom. The current basic roles are Admin, Writer and Reader (roles/admin, roles/writer, roles/reader); Owner, Editor and Viewer are the legacy basic roles. Both sets are broad and discouraged in production, so prefer a predefined role that matches the job, such as Compute Viewer or Logs Viewer.

concepts.heading: Workforce Identity Federation
concepts.body: When employees or partners already sign in with an external identity provider such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, Workforce Identity Federation lets them use the Google Cloud console and gcloud with single sign-on without creating or syncing any Cloud Identity accounts. You create a workforce identity pool at the organization level (`gcloud iam workforce-pools create corp-pool --organization=ORG_ID --location=global`), add an OIDC or SAML 2.0 provider with attribute mappings such as google.subject and google.groups, and grant roles to pool principals. Because federated users have no Google email, bindings use identifiers like principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/corp-pool/group/sre-team for everyone in an IdP group, or principal://.../subject/SUBJECT for one person. Do not confuse it with Workload Identity Federation, which is for applications and pipelines, not people.

concepts.heading: Seeing What You Have: Cloud Asset Inventory and Gemini Cloud Assist
concepts.body: Cloud Asset Inventory is a metadata inventory of resources and IAM policies across a project, folder or organization. Search answers quick questions interactively, for example `gcloud asset search-all-resources --scope=organizations/ORG_ID --asset-types=compute.googleapis.com/Instance --query='labels.env:*'`. Export writes a snapshot to Cloud Storage or BigQuery for bulk analysis. History returns how an asset changed over the last 35 days. Feeds publish future changes to a Pub/Sub topic in near real time. The Cloud Asset Inventory API must be enabled in the project you run commands from. Gemini Cloud Assist is the AI assistant in the console; besides general help it can list resources, recent changes and role holders, and shows a query you can run to verify. For resource questions it needs the Gemini Cloud Assist API and the Cloud Asset Inventory API enabled, and users need Gemini Cloud Assist User plus Cloud Asset Viewer.

examPoints: A question that keeps users and groups in step with Active Directory and lets people sign in with their AD passwords is testing GCDS for one-way provisioning plus SAML SSO for authentication.

A question about giving a group access without disturbing existing grants is testing add-iam-policy-binding; set-iam-policy replaces the whole policy, and basic roles (current or legacy) are rarely the best answer for production.

A question about people signing in through an external IdP with no account sync is testing Workforce Identity Federation, while inventory questions separate search, export, 35-day history and Pub/Sub feeds.

quiz.q: An engineer wanted to give a new group read access to project web-prod. He saved a JSON file containing only that group's binding and ran gcloud projects set-iam-policy web-prod with it. Shortly afterwards several teams lost access to the project. What happened?
choices: The new binding conflicted with older grants, so IAM disabled them until an administrator approves the change
The command replaced the whole allow policy with the file, so every binding missing from it was removed
The group was granted a legacy basic role, which automatically removes predefined roles held by other principals
The project inherits its policy from the folder, so any project-level change resets inherited grants to empty
quiz.explain: set-iam-policy overwrites the entire policy, so bindings left out of the file are deleted; add-iam-policy-binding adds a single binding safely. Choice D is tempting because inheritance matters elsewhere, but inherited grants come from the folder and are not reset by a project change.

quiz.q: Someone changed the metadata of a VM about three weeks ago and the application has misbehaved since. No one recorded the old values. Which tool can show what the VM's configuration looked like before the change?
choices: A Cloud Asset Inventory feed created today on the VM's asset type, which publishes its earlier states to Pub/Sub
A Cloud Asset Inventory export to BigQuery, which writes a snapshot that includes every earlier version of the VM
gcloud asset search-all-resources with the VM's name, which returns each saved revision of the resource's metadata
Cloud Asset Inventory asset history for the VM, which keeps create, update and delete changes for 35 days
quiz.explain: Asset history keeps changes for 35 days, so a three-week-old state is still available. Choice A is tempting because feeds track changes, but a feed only reports changes that happen after it is created.

days.recap: People come from Cloud Identity (by hand or via one-way GCDS sync with SAML SSO) or from an external IdP through Workforce Identity Federation; grant predefined roles to groups with add-iam-policy-binding, and use Cloud Asset Inventory and Gemini Cloud Assist to see what exists.

days.title: Project Setup: APIs, Quotas, Locations, Observability Metrics Scopes and the First Network

concepts.heading: Enabling APIs
concepts.body: A Google Cloud service can be used in a project only after its API is enabled there. Use APIs & Services in the console or `gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com run.googleapis.com --project=PROJECT`, and list what is possible with `gcloud services list --available`. Enabling and disabling need the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin); Service Usage Consumer only lets someone use services that are already enabled, and Service Usage Viewer only reads their state. Disabling an API is not a cleanup and its effect depends on the service: Cloud Storage and BigQuery data stay, and keep being billed; Cloud Run resources are deleted; GKE clusters are suspended and deleted after 30 days unless the API is enabled again. Charges already incurred are still billed. Take an inventory of a service's resources, for example with Cloud Asset Inventory, before turning its API off.

concepts.heading: Quotas and Increase Requests
concepts.body: Cloud Quotas protects shared capacity by limiting how much of each resource a project can use. Most quotas are per project and many are regional or zonal, so CPUs in us-central1 are counted separately from CPUs in europe-west1. Allocation quotas (such as number of VMs) free up when you delete resources, rate quotas (requests per minute or per day) reset when the period resets, and concurrent quotas limit operations running at the same time. System limits, such as maximum sizes, are fixed and cannot be raised. When a deployment fails with a quota error, open IAM & Admin, Quotas & System Limits, filter to the quota and region, choose Edit quota and submit a new value with a justification; you need Quota Administrator (roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin), and no paid support plan. For steadily growing projects the quota adjuster can request modest increases automatically when peak usage gets close to the value.

concepts.heading: Regions, Zones and Product Availability
concepts.body: A region is an independent geographic area such as europe-west4, and a zone is a deployment area inside it such as europe-west4-b. Zonal resources (VMs, zonal disks) fail with their zone, regional resources (static external IPs, regional disks) span zones, and some resources (images) are global. Product availability is not uniform: machine series, GPUs and TPUs exist only in certain zones, so check before you pick a location. `gcloud compute machine-types list --filter='name=c4d-standard-4'` returns one row per zone that offers the type, `gcloud compute accelerator-types list` shows GPU types by zone, and `gcloud compute regions describe us-central1` shows a region's details including its regional quotas. Choose regions close to users and data, and check data residency requirements, which may also be enforced with the resource locations organization policy.

concepts.heading: Provisioning Google Cloud Observability: Metrics Scopes
concepts.body: Google Cloud Observability includes Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging. Each project stores the metrics of its own resources, and its metrics scope lists the projects whose data it can chart and alert on; by default that is only itself. To watch several projects in one place, Google recommends a dedicated scoping project without its own resources, for example ops-central, and adding shop-staging and shop-prod to its metrics scope under Monitoring Settings. The scoping project stores the dashboards, alerting policies and uptime checks. Changing a metrics scope requires Monitoring Admin on the scoping project and on every project added or removed; viewing the combined data needs only Monitoring Viewer on the scoping project, which means that viewer sees every project in the scope, so give different teams different scoping projects. For metrics from inside a VM, such as memory use, install the Ops Agent on the VM.

concepts.heading: The First Network
concepts.body: Unless disabled, every new project gets a default network: an auto mode VPC with one subnet in each region from predefined ranges inside 10.128.0.0/9, plus firewall rules such as default-allow-internal, SSH and RDP. That is handy for experiments but risky for production: the ranges often overlap on-premises networks, and auto mode networks cannot be connected to each other with VPC Network Peering or Cloud VPN because their ranges are identical. Production projects use custom mode networks, where you choose regions and ranges: `gcloud compute networks create prod-vpc --subnet-mode=custom`, then `gcloud compute networks subnets create prod-ew1 --network=prod-vpc --region=europe-west1 --range=10.20.0.0/20`. You can convert an auto mode network to custom mode, but never back. Setting the boolean constraint compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation on a folder makes every new project in it start with no network.

examPoints: A question about a developer who cannot turn on an API is testing Service Usage Admin versus Consumer, and a question about turning an API off checks that data may stay, be deleted or be suspended depending on the service.
A question that fails on a regional quota is answered by an adjustment request for that quota and region in Quotas & System Limits, not by a support plan or by moving to another project.

A question about monitoring several projects together is testing metrics scopes: an empty scoping project, Monitoring Admin on both sides to change the scope, Monitoring Viewer on the scoping project to view.

quiz.q: A data-loading script calls an API in a tight loop and fails with an error that a requests-per-minute quota was exceeded. When the engineer reruns it a minute later, the first calls succeed again. What best explains this behavior?
choices: It is an allocation quota, so capacity was released only when the script's earlier calls deleted their resources
It is a system limit, so the value is fixed by Google and the script hit the absolute maximum for the service
It is a concurrent quota, so it counts only long-running operations that are still in progress at the same time
It is a rate quota, so usage is counted per time period and the allowance resets when the next period begins
quiz.explain: Rate quotas limit usage per time period and reset with it, which is why the calls work again a minute later. Choice A is tempting because allocation quotas also free up, but only when resources are deleted, not with time.

quiz.q: A team built a test environment in a project's default network. They now want to stop new subnets from appearing automatically when Google adds regions and want to choose all future subnet ranges themselves, without rebuilding the VMs already running. What should they do?
choices: Convert the auto mode network to custom mode, which keeps existing subnets and adds new ones only by hand
Enforce compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation on the project, which turns the existing default network into custom mode
Peer the default network with a new custom mode network, so that new regions take their ranges from the custom one
Delete the default-allow-internal firewall rule, because that rule is what creates subnets in newly added regions
quiz.explain: An auto mode network can be converted to custom mode in place, and from then on subnets are created only when you add them. Choice B is tempting because the constraint is about default networks, but it only skips creating one in new projects and does not change an existing network.

days.recap: Enable APIs with Service Usage Admin and inventory before disabling, raise regional quotas through Quotas & System Limits, check machine and accelerator availability per zone, monitor many projects through a resource-free scoping project's metrics scope, and give production custom mode VPCs instead of the auto mode default network.

days.title: Billing: Billing Accounts and Roles, Linking Projects, Budgets and Spend Caps, Export to BigQuery

concepts.heading: Cloud Billing Accounts
concepts.body: A Cloud Billing account defines who pays for a set of projects, and a project can use paid services only while it is linked to an active billing account. Every new billing account starts as self-serve (online): it is paid by credit or debit card, or direct debit where available, and charged automatically each month or when a threshold is reached. An invoiced (offline) account receives a monthly invoice paid by check or wire transfer within agreed terms. You cannot switch an account to invoiced yourself: a Billing Account Administrator of the current account applies, and Google checks eligibility such as how long the business has been registered and expected spend. One billing account usually pays for many projects, and billing roles are granted on the billing account (or on the organization for all its billing accounts), not on individual projects, which keeps invoices and payment details away from project teams.

concepts.heading: Billing Roles
concepts.body: The predefined Cloud Billing roles separate duties. Billing Account Creator (roles/billing.creator), granted at the organization, creates new billing accounts. Billing Account Administrator (roles/billing.admin) owns an account: payment methods, project links, exports and access for others. Billing Account Costs Manager (roles/billing.costsManager) creates budgets, views costs and manages the cost export to BigQuery, but cannot link projects or manage account access. Billing Account Viewer (roles/billing.viewer) reads costs and transactions, typically for finance. Billing Account User (roles/billing.user) only lets someone link projects to the account, so it can be granted widely; together with Project Creator on a folder it lets developers create projects paid by the central account without seeing invoices. Project Billing Manager (roles/billing.projectManager) is granted on a project and lets someone link or unlink that project without access to its resources.

concepts.heading: Linking, Moving and Locking Project Billing
concepts.body: Changing a project's billing link needs permission on both sides: on the project (Project Billing Manager or Owner) and on the target billing account (Billing Account User or Administrator). `gcloud billing projects link web-prod --billing-account=0X0X0X-0X0X0X-0X0X0X` links a project, and if it is already linked elsewhere the same command moves it without downtime. Charges before the move stay with the old account and later ones go to the new account, so a month can be split between two invoices. `gcloud billing projects unlink web-prod` disables billing: every service in the project stops, some resources may be deleted, and on a Shared VPC host project the VMs in attached service projects lose their network and shut down. `gcloud billing projects describe` shows the current link. To protect a critical project, lock its billing link; a locked link cannot be moved or removed until someone deliberately unlocks it.

concepts.heading: Budgets, Alerts and Spend Caps
concepts.body: An alerts-only budget tracks spend against an amount for a monthly, quarterly, yearly or custom period, scoped to the whole billing account or to projects, folders, services or resource labels (project labels are not available as a filter). Threshold rules default to 50%, 90% and 100% of actual spend; a forecasted rule warns early when the end-of-period forecast will pass the threshold, but forecasts need a calendar period, not a custom range. Alert emails go to Billing Account Administrators and Users by default; add other people with Cloud Monitoring email channels. A connected Pub/Sub topic receives status messages several times a day, and code such as a Cloud Run function can act on costAmount versus budgetAmount, for example by disabling billing. Alerts-only budgets never stop spending themselves. A spend cap budget does pause usage, but only for one project and one eligible service (Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions), monthly, and never persistent resources such as VMs and disks.

concepts.heading: Billing Export to BigQuery
concepts.body: For analysis with SQL, enable Cloud Billing export to a BigQuery dataset, ideally in a separate FinOps project linked to the same billing account. Each export is enabled separately. The standard usage cost export holds services, SKUs, projects, labels, credits and costs, which suits trends. The detailed usage cost export adds resource-level rows, so you can find which VM or disk drives a rise. The pricing export lists the account's prices and needs Billing Account Administrator plus the BigQuery Data Transfer Service API in the dataset's project; cost exports can be set up by a Costs Manager or Administrator with BigQuery User on that project. Location matters: a dataset in the US or EU multi-region is backfilled from the start of the previous month, while a regional dataset starts on the day you enable the export, and a dataset's location can never change. Data is not retroactive for pricing.

examPoints: A question that lets people attach projects to a billing account without seeing invoices is testing Billing Account User, while budgets and cost export without link control is Billing Account Costs Manager.

A question about moving a project between billing accounts is testing that `gcloud billing projects link` moves it with no gap, that earlier charges stay on the old account, and that unlinking disables billing and stops services.

A question that must stop costs automatically is testing that alerts-only budgets only notify; either automate a response through Pub/Sub or, for one eligible API service in one project, use a spend cap budget.

quiz.q: A team runs a hackathon project where participants call Cloud Run heavily. They want Cloud Run usage in that one project to pause automatically once the month's estimated Cloud Run costs pass a set amount, while two Compute Engine VMs in the same project keep running. What should they configure?
choices: An alerts-only budget on the project with a 100% actual threshold, which pauses every paid service once it fires
A Cloud Run quota decrease in Quotas & System Limits, which tracks the cost amount and blocks requests above it
A monthly spend cap budget scoped to the project and the Cloud Run service, which pauses only that service's usage
A Pub/Sub budget notification wired to a function that unlinks billing, which pauses only Cloud Run in the project
quiz.explain: A spend cap budget covers one project and one eligible service such as Cloud Run, pauses that service's new usage and leaves persistent resources like VMs running. Choice D is tempting because it is the documented automation, but disabling billing stops every service in the project, including the VMs.

quiz.q: Finance enables the detailed usage cost export to a new BigQuery dataset in the europe-west3 region. They are surprised that the tables contain no costs from before that day, although the billing account has been in use for a year. Why?
choices: A regional dataset gets data only from the day the export is enabled; US or EU multi-regions are backfilled
The detailed export never contains historical data; only the standard export is backfilled to the previous month
Historical rows appear only after the pricing export is also enabled in the same dataset of the FinOps project
The dataset's project must be linked to a different billing account than the exported one before any backfill can start
quiz.explain: A US or EU multi-region dataset gets data from the start of the previous month, while a regional dataset starts on the enable date, and the location cannot be changed later. Choice B is tempting because the two exports differ in detail, but the backfill depends on the dataset location, not on the export type.

days.recap: Billing accounts are self-serve or invoiced, billing roles split owning, viewing, cost tools and linking, project links need roles on both sides and can be locked, alerts-only budgets notify while spend caps pause one eligible service, and exports to a US or EU dataset bring last month's costs into BigQuery.

days.title: Choosing Compute and Launching VMs: Machine Types, Availability Policy, Spot VMs and Disks

concepts.heading: Choosing Where Code Runs
concepts.body: The compute services differ in how much of the stack you control. Compute Engine gives you virtual machines with full control of the guest OS, kernel modules and drivers, so it suits lift-and-shift of software that must run unmodified on an operating system. GKE runs containers on managed Kubernetes; in Autopilot Google manages the nodes. Cloud Run runs stateless containers that answer requests or run jobs, scales out with traffic and scales to zero when idle, so an unused service with no minimum instances costs nothing for CPU and memory. Cloud Run functions deploy a single function from source and run on Cloud Run. Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine) is a managed runtime for AI agents with sessions, long-term Memory Bank and built-in tracing. On the exam, the phrases 'kernel driver' or 'full OS' mean Compute Engine, 'no infrastructure and nothing when idle' means Cloud Run.

concepts.heading: Machine Types: Predefined and Custom
concepts.body: A machine type sets vCPUs and memory. Predefined types such as n2-standard-8 (8 vCPUs, 32 GB) cover most needs. When none fits, for example software licensed per vCPU that needs 6 vCPUs and 30 GB, create a custom machine type: `gcloud compute instances create risk-1 --zone=us-central1-a --custom-vm-type=n2 --custom-cpu=6 --custom-memory=30GB`. Custom types exist only for the general-purpose N and E series (such as N4, N2, N2D, E2, N1) and the accelerator-optimized G2 series, not for C series or Tau. Each series has a memory-per-vCPU range, 0.5 to 8 GB for N2; to go beyond it on N-series types, enable extended memory with `--custom-extensions`, which E2 does not support. Before choosing a zone, check that the machine series is offered there with `gcloud compute machine-types list --filter`. Custom types cost a little more than an equal predefined type but can save much more on per-vCPU licenses.

concepts.heading: Availability Policy: Maintenance and Restart
concepts.body: Each VM has a host maintenance policy. Maintenance behavior (onHostMaintenance) is MIGRATE, which live-migrates the running VM to another host so it keeps running, or TERMINATE, which stops it. Restart behavior (automaticRestart, default true) restarts a VM that was stopped by a host error, crash or terminate-on-maintenance event. Most machine types default to MIGRATE with automatic restart. VMs with attached GPUs cannot live migrate, so they must use TERMINATE, and automatic restart brings them back afterwards. A script with `--maintenance-policy=TERMINATE --no-restart-on-failure` on an ordinary VM leaves it stopped after the next maintenance event until someone starts it. You can change the host maintenance policy of an existing VM. When a question says a VM must keep running through Google's maintenance, the answer is MIGRATE with automatic restart left on.

concepts.heading: Spot VMs
concepts.body: Spot VMs use the spot provisioning model: they run on spare Compute Engine capacity at a large discount, and Compute Engine can preempt them at any time to reclaim it. They are the newer version of preemptible VMs, which are always stopped after 24 hours; Spot VMs have no such limit unless you set a maximum run duration. Spot VMs cannot live migrate, cannot restart automatically and are outside the Compute Engine SLA. On preemption the termination action applies: STOP (default) leaves the VM TERMINATED with its disks still billed, while DELETE removes it, for example `gcloud compute instances create worker-1 --provisioning-model=SPOT --instance-termination-action=DELETE`. Local SSD data is not kept through preemption. Spot VMs fit fault-tolerant, retryable work such as batch rendering or queue workers, especially inside a managed instance group that recreates preempted VMs automatically.

concepts.heading: Disks: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Local SSD
concepts.body: Compute Engine block storage is durable or temporary. Durable volumes, Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk, are network-attached, survive VM deletion if you keep them, can be detached and reattached, and are the only choice for boot disks. Persistent Disk performance grows with size, so more IOPS means a bigger disk; it is not available on the latest machine series. Hyperdisk sets size and performance independently: Hyperdisk Balanced for most databases, Extreme for the highest IOPS, Throughput for streaming workloads, ML for read-only data shared by many VMs. Zonal disks live in one zone; regional Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability replicate writes synchronously to two zones, so a zone loss loses no acknowledged data. Local SSD is physically attached to the host, fastest, lost by default when the VM stops or fails, never a boot disk, and can only be added when the VM is created. Use it for scratch data and caches.

examPoints: A question about software licensed per vCPU or an odd vCPU-to-memory ratio is testing custom machine types on N or E series, with extended memory for more than 8 GB per vCPU on N series.
A question about a VM that stayed down after maintenance, or a GPU VM that cannot be created with live migration, is testing onHostMaintenance (MIGRATE or TERMINATE) and automaticRestart.
A question that needs zone-failure protection with no data loss is testing regional Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability; Local SSD and snapshots cannot give that.

quiz.q: An engineer creates a VM with one attached GPU, using a script that also sets --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE. The create request fails with an error about the host maintenance setting. What should the engineer change?
choices: Set the maintenance policy to TERMINATE, because VMs with attached GPUs cannot live migrate during host maintenance
Remove the GPU and attach it after the VM starts, because GPUs can only be added to a VM that is already running
Switch the VM to the spot provisioning model, because only Spot VMs can be live migrated while a GPU is attached
Add --no-restart-on-failure to the script, because automatic restart conflicts with migration for every GPU type
quiz.explain: GPUs are tied to specific hardware, so VMs with GPUs must use TERMINATE for host maintenance; automatic restart can stay on. Choice C is tempting because Spot VMs are common for GPU work, but Spot VMs cannot live migrate at all.

quiz.q: A cache server runs on a VM that was created without Local SSD. The team now wants to add a Local SSD disk to it for faster scratch space. What should they do?
choices: Stop the VM, attach a Local SSD disk in the console and start it again, because Local SSD can be added while stopped
Attach a Local SSD disk while the VM is running, because Local SSD is hot-pluggable on all current machine series
Create a new VM with Local SSD defined at creation and move the cache, because Local SSD cannot be added later
Resize the boot disk to Local SSD, because a durable boot volume can be converted to Local SSD while the VM is stopped
quiz.explain: Local SSD disks can only be added when a VM is created, so the cache must move to a new VM that includes them. Choice A is tempting because many disk changes are done on stopped VMs, but that applies to durable disks, not Local SSD.

days.recap: Pick Compute Engine for OS control, GKE for Kubernetes, Cloud Run or Cloud Run functions for serverless and Agent Runtime for AI agents; size VMs with predefined or custom types, set the maintenance and restart policy deliberately, use Spot VMs for retryable work, and choose Hyperdisk, Persistent Disk (zonal or regional) or temporary Local SSD by durability and performance needs.

days.title: VM Fleets: Instance Templates, Managed Instance Groups, Autoscaling and Autohealing, OS Login, VM Manager, GPUs and TPUs

concepts.heading: Instance Templates and Managed Instance Groups
concepts.body: An instance template saves a VM configuration: machine type, boot image, disks, network, labels, metadata and startup script. A managed instance group (MIG) is always created from a template and builds every VM from it, which gives you identical, replaceable VMs. Templates are immutable: to change the machine type or image you create a new template (often based on the old one) and roll it out to the MIG, for example with a rolling update that replaces VMs gradually. Editing a VM in a MIG by hand is a trap, because the MIG recreates VMs from the template whenever it repairs, scales or updates them. A zonal MIG keeps its VMs in one zone; a regional MIG spreads them across zones of a region (three by default), so the group keeps serving when one zone fails. A MIG also recreates VMs that crash, are deleted or are preempted, which pairs well with Spot VMs for cheap, self-healing workers.

concepts.heading: Autoscaling and Autohealing
concepts.body: The MIG autoscaler adds and removes VMs based on signals such as average CPU utilization, load balancing serving capacity or Cloud Monitoring metrics. The initialization period (60 seconds by default) tells it to ignore new VMs that are still starting up when deciding to scale out; set it to the app's real start time or busy booting VMs cause overshoot. The stabilization period (10 minutes) keeps enough VMs for the peak seen in that window before scaling in, and scale-in controls limit how fast the group shrinks. A group scaling on CPU, serving capacity or per-VM metrics can never reach zero; a metric from outside the VMs, such as a Pub/Sub subscription backlog, can, with the minimum set to 0. Autohealing is separate: attach an application health check to the MIG, and it recreates VMs whose app stops answering. Use a conservative autohealing check, distinct from the load balancer's check, which only steers traffic.

concepts.heading: SSH Access: OS Login and Metadata Keys
concepts.body: Linux VMs accept SSH in two ways. Metadata-based keys are public keys stored in project or instance metadata; everyone connecting that way gets sudo, keys must be removed by hand, and anyone who can edit project metadata can reach every VM that does not block project keys. Setting `block-project-ssh-keys=TRUE` on one VM's metadata limits it to its own keys. OS Login, recommended in most cases, ties SSH to the user's Google identity and checks IAM on every login. Turn it on with the metadata key `enable-oslogin=TRUE` on the project or on individual VMs, then grant roles/compute.osLogin for login without sudo or roles/compute.osAdminLogin for login with sudo, on the project or on a single instance. Removing the role removes access immediately, and OS Login supports 2-step verification and audit logging, which is why exam scenarios about contractors and revocation point to it.

concepts.heading: VM Manager
concepts.body: VM Manager manages operating systems across large Compute Engine fleets. It needs the OS Config API enabled and the OS Config agent running on each VM, and it has three parts. Patch runs patch jobs on demand or on a schedule, with pre- and post-patch scripts and compliance reports. OS inventory management collects installed packages and OS versions so you can review them. OS policies declare a desired state, such as a package that must be installed or removed on all VMs with a label, and the agent keeps enforcing it, so a package someone removes comes back without a reboot, unlike a startup script that runs only at boot. Patch does not host packages: the agent calls the OS's own package manager, such as apt on Ubuntu, so VMs without external IPs need Cloud NAT, a proxy or a local repository, even though their inventory and compliance data still reach Google APIs.

concepts.heading: GPUs versus TPUs
concepts.body: Accelerators speed up machine learning and other parallel work. GPUs attach to Compute Engine VMs and GKE nodes, are available only in certain zones (check with `gcloud compute accelerator-types list`) and make the VM use the TERMINATE maintenance policy. TPUs are Google's custom ASICs for ML, built for large matrix operations with high-bandwidth on-chip memory, connected in slices to scale; code is compiled by XLA, and you use them through Compute Engine, GKE or Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Google's guidance: CPUs for quick prototypes, small models and I/O-bound work; GPUs for medium to large models with custom PyTorch or JAX operations or ops not supported on TPUs; TPUs for models dominated by matrix math with no custom operations in the training loop, long training runs with large batches, and ultra-large embeddings for ranking and recommendation. Frequent branching or high-precision arithmetic points away from TPUs.

examPoints: A question that wants to change the machine type of a MIG is testing that templates are immutable: create a new template and roll it out, never edit the old template or a single VM.

A question about overshooting scale-out, a group that never reaches zero, or VMs whose app hangs is testing the initialization period, external metrics with a minimum of 0, and an autohealing health check on the MIG.

A question about IAM-controlled SSH that is revoked when a role is removed is testing OS Login, with osLogin for no sudo and osAdminLogin for sudo; VM Manager questions separate Patch, inventory and OS policies.

quiz.q: A project uses OS Login, and contractors hold roles/compute.osLogin on the project. One contractor now needs to run commands with sudo on a single VM, build-01, and nowhere else. What should the engineer grant?
choices: roles/compute.osAdminLogin on the project, because OS Login roles can only be granted at the project level or above
roles/compute.osAdminLogin on the build-01 instance, because that role adds sudo and can be granted on one VM
roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 on build-01, because the instance admin role adds sudo to existing OS Login access
Add the contractor's SSH key to build-01's metadata, because metadata keys work alongside OS Login and give sudo
quiz.explain: roles/compute.osAdminLogin grants login with sudo and can be granted on a single instance, which keeps the access narrow. Choice A is tempting because the existing role sits on the project, but OS Login roles can also be granted at the instance level, and a project grant would give sudo on every VM.

quiz.q: A MIG autoscales on CPU utilization. After a short traffic peak the CPU drops right away, yet the group keeps its extra VMs for several more minutes before deleting them. The team asks whether something is broken. What explains the delay?
choices: The initialization period keeps new VMs out of every scale-in decision until they have run for ten full minutes
The autohealing health check is still marking the extra VMs as healthy, which blocks the autoscaler from removing them
The group is regional, and a regional MIG may only remove VMs after each zone reports the same CPU level for an hour
The stabilization period keeps enough VMs for the peak load seen over the last 10 minutes before the group scales in
quiz.explain: The autoscaler deliberately keeps capacity for the peak observed during the stabilization period, about 10 minutes, so short dips do not cause churn. Choice A is tempting because the initialization period is the other timing setting, but it affects scale-out decisions about starting VMs, not scale-in.

days.recap: Build fleets from immutable instance templates in zonal or regional MIGs, tune autoscaling with the initialization and stabilization periods, use autohealing health checks for hung apps, control SSH with OS Login roles, keep OS state with VM Manager, and choose CPUs, GPUs or TPUs by model shape.

days.title: Google Kubernetes Engine: Autopilot and Standard, Regional and Private Clusters, kubectl, Deploying Apps and Release Channels

concepts.heading: Autopilot and Standard
concepts.body: GKE has two modes. In Autopilot, the recommended mode, Google manages the infrastructure: it provisions and scales nodes from your Pod specifications, applies security settings and handles upgrades. You deploy Kubernetes manifests and request special hardware such as GPUs through ComputeClasses rather than node pools. General-purpose Autopilot Pods are billed for the resources the Pods request; Pods that select specific hardware use node-based billing, the hardware plus a management premium. Autopilot clusters are always regional and always in a release channel. In Standard mode you create and manage node pools yourself, choosing machine types, node autoscaling and upgrade settings, and you pay for the nodes whether Pods use them or not. Choose Autopilot for a team that does not want to size or repair nodes, and Standard when the scenario needs direct control of node configuration.

concepts.heading: Zonal and Regional Clusters
concepts.body: A zonal cluster has a single control plane in one zone. If that zone has an outage you cannot deploy, scale or reconfigure workloads until it returns, even if nodes in other zones keep running. A regional cluster runs control plane replicas in several zones of the region, and by default replicates each node pool across three zones, so it survives the loss of a zone. Google recommends regional clusters for production. The availability type is fixed at creation: a zonal cluster cannot become regional, or the reverse, so changing it means creating a new cluster and migrating workloads. When creating a Standard cluster from the CLI, `--location` takes a zone for a zonal cluster or a region for a regional one, for example `gcloud container clusters create shop --location=us-central1`. Autopilot clusters are created with `gcloud container clusters create-auto` and are regional.

concepts.heading: Private Nodes and Egress
concepts.body: Security rules often forbid external IP addresses on nodes. With `--enable-private-nodes`, GKE gives nodes internal IP addresses only. Private Google Access is turned on automatically for the subnet (unless you use Shared VPC), so nodes can still pull images from Artifact Registry and reach other Google APIs. Nodes have no path to the internet by themselves, so to pull images from a public registry or call a partner's HTTPS API you add Cloud NAT, which lets resources without external IPs open outbound connections while accepting no inbound ones. A separate control is authorized networks, which limit which source IP ranges can reach the cluster's control plane endpoint; they do nothing for node egress. On the exam, separate three needs: no external IPs on nodes (private nodes), outbound internet (Cloud NAT) and Google APIs from private nodes (Private Google Access).

concepts.heading: kubectl and Deploying a Containerized App
concepts.body: kubectl is the Kubernetes CLI. Cloud Shell already has it; on your own machine run `gcloud components install kubectl` and `gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`, because kubectl gets its short-lived GKE credentials through that plugin and fails without it. Then `gcloud container clusters get-credentials shop --location=us-central1` writes the cluster's kubeconfig entry. To run an image from Artifact Registry, `kubectl create deployment web --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/repo/web:1.0` creates a Deployment that keeps the desired number of Pods running and replaces failed ones. Pods are not reachable from outside by default: `kubectl expose deployment web --type LoadBalancer --port 80 --target-port 8080` creates a Service backed by a Google Cloud load balancer, where --port is what clients use and --target-port is where the container listens. Without --type the Service is ClusterIP, reachable only inside the cluster. `kubectl get service web` shows the external IP.

concepts.heading: Release Channels
concepts.body: Release channels decide how quickly GKE moves a cluster to new versions. Rapid gets new Kubernetes releases a week or two after upstream general availability and suits testing in pre-production. Regular, the default and the one Google recommends for most users, gets versions about two months after Rapid. Stable gets them later still, after validation in the other channels, for teams that value stability over new features. Extended follows Regular's timing but lets a cluster stay on a minor version for as long as possible, for long-term support. Not enrolling in a channel (No channel) is deprecated, and Autopilot clusters are always enrolled. GKE auto-upgrades enrolled clusters, and critical security patches reach every channel. To hold a cluster on a version for a while, for example during a sales peak, Google recommends maintenance exclusions rather than leaving the channel. A common pattern is pre-production on Rapid or Regular and production on Regular or Stable.

examPoints: A question about a small team that does not want to manage nodes and wants to pay for what Pods request is testing Autopilot; full control of node pools points to Standard.
A question that needs the control plane to survive a zone loss is testing regional clusters and the rule that zonal or regional is fixed at creation.

A question about nodes without external IPs that still need the internet is testing private nodes plus Cloud NAT, and a question about kubectl failing on a new laptop is testing gke-gcloud-auth-plugin and get-credentials.

quiz.q: An engineer deploys an image to GKE with kubectl create deployment and then runs kubectl expose deployment web --port 80 --target-port 8080. Other Pods in the cluster can reach the app, but users on the internet cannot, and the Service has no external IP. Why?
choices: The target port must equal the Service port, so the Service waits for the container to listen on port 80 first
The Deployment has only one replica, and GKE assigns an external IP only after a Deployment has three replicas
The cluster uses private nodes, so no Service of any type can receive an external IP address on this cluster
Without a --type flag the Service is ClusterIP, which is reachable only inside the cluster; use type LoadBalancer
quiz.explain: ClusterIP is the default Service type and gives a stable internal IP only; --type LoadBalancer makes GKE provision an external load balancer. Choice C is tempting because private nodes sound related, but they remove external IPs from nodes, not from a LoadBalancer Service.

quiz.q: A regulated team runs a GKE cluster whose workloads are certified on one Kubernetes minor version. They want the cluster to stay on that minor version for as long as GKE supports it, while still being enrolled in a release channel. Which channel fits best?
choices: Stable, because clusters in Stable never receive automatic upgrades to a newer minor version once they are created
Extended, because it lets a cluster keep running a minor version for as long as possible with long-term support
Rapid, because it receives security patches first, so the cluster can safely stay on its current minor version
No channel, because leaving every release channel is the recommended way to pin a cluster to one minor version
quiz.explain: The Extended channel is meant for long-term support, keeping a cluster on a minor version as long as possible. Choice A is tempting because Stable is the slowest of the regular channels, but Stable clusters are still auto-upgraded to newer minor versions.

days.recap: Autopilot manages nodes and bills by Pod requests while Standard gives node pool control, regional clusters survive a zone loss and the choice is fixed at creation, private nodes need Cloud NAT for the internet, kubectl needs the auth plugin and get-credentials, a LoadBalancer Service publishes a Deployment, and release channels set the upgrade pace with Regular as the default.

days.title: Serverless Deployment and Events: Cloud Run, Cloud Run Functions, Public Access, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage Events and Eventarc

concepts.heading: Deploying a Cloud Run Service
concepts.body: Cloud Run deploys containers without servers to manage. `gcloud run deploy web --image=europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/repo/web:1.0 --region=europe-west1` deploys an image you built. `gcloud run deploy web --source . --region=europe-west1` deploys from a folder: Cloud Build uses the Dockerfile if there is one, or Google Cloud's buildpacks if not, and stores the image in an Artifact Registry repository named cloud-run-source-deploy, so Docker is not needed locally. The container contract matters: the ingress container must listen on 0.0.0.0 on the port in the PORT variable (8080 by default), and Cloud Run terminates TLS, so the app serves plain HTTP. The file system is in memory and not shared, so keep instances stateless and put data in Cloud Storage or a database. A service answers requests at an endpoint; a Cloud Run job runs to completion with no port, and can run many parallel tasks.

concepts.heading: Cloud Run Functions
concepts.body: Cloud Run functions, formerly Cloud Functions, deploy a single function from source and run it as a Cloud Run service. The current docs deploy them with the same command as services: `gcloud run deploy handle-order --source . --function process_order --base-image BASE_IMAGE --region europe-west1`. The `--function` flag names the entry point, the function in your code that Cloud Run executes, so it must match the function name exactly. The `--base-image` flag picks a Google-managed language runtime image that receives automatic security updates. Functions created earlier with `gcloud functions deploy` are still supported for backward compatibility. After deployment you attach triggers such as Eventarc to react to events, or call the function over HTTPS. Choose a function for one small handler, a service for a whole web app or full control of the container.

concepts.heading: Public Access and the Invoker Check
concepts.body: By default Cloud Run requires every caller to hold the Cloud Run Invoker role (roles/run.invoker), which suits internal APIs and event targets. To make a service public there are two ways. The recommended one is to disable the Invoker IAM check: `gcloud run deploy web --no-invoker-iam-check` for a new service or `gcloud run services update web --no-invoker-iam-check` for an existing one, and `--invoker-iam-check` turns it back on. The older way grants roles/run.invoker to allUsers, which is what `--allow-unauthenticated` does; organizations with the Domain restricted sharing constraint, part of the security baseline, reject that grant, so disabling the check is the documented answer there. Administrators can forbid disabling the check with the managed constraint run.managed.requireInvokerIam. Changing the setting needs run.services.setIamPolicy, included in Cloud Run Admin. Event-triggered services stay private and grant Invoker to the trigger's service account.

concepts.heading: Processing Pub/Sub Messages
concepts.body: Pub/Sub decouples producers from consumers. To have messages delivered to a private Cloud Run service, create a push subscription to the service URL with an authentication service account: `gcloud pubsub subscriptions create orders-push --topic=orders --push-endpoint=SERVICE_URL --push-auth-service-account=invoker-sa@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and grant that account roles/run.invoker on the service. Pub/Sub attaches a token for that account and Cloud Run checks it. The HTTP response acknowledges the message: a success code such as 200 or 204 acks it, while an error code such as 500 makes Pub/Sub deliver it again, so a handler that always fails on one bad message sees it over and over. Delivery is at least once, so handlers should be idempotent. Alternatively, an Eventarc trigger of type google.cloud.pubsub.topic.v1.messagePublished with --transport-topic set to an existing topic delivers the messages as CloudEvents.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Events and Eventarc
concepts.body: Eventarc routes events to Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions, GKE services, Workflows and HTTP endpoints in CloudEvents format. Eventarc Standard uses triggers for one source to one destination; Eventarc Advanced adds a central bus, enrollments, cross-project delivery and transformation for many teams. Cloud Storage sends direct events: object.v1.finalized for new or overwritten objects, metadataUpdated, archived and deleted. A trigger filters on the type and the bucket, and must be created in the bucket's location: `gcloud eventarc triggers create uploads --location=europe-west4 --destination-run-service=thumbs --event-filters=type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized --event-filters=bucket=inv-in --service-account=SA_EMAIL`. Grant the Cloud Storage service agent roles/pubsub.publisher, and the trigger's account roles/eventarc.eventReceiver plus invoke rights. Triggers on Cloud Audit Logs (google.cloud.audit.log.v1.written) cover other services, but data operations fire only after Data Access audit logs are enabled.

examPoints: A question about a revision that never becomes ready is often testing the container contract: listen on 0.0.0.0 at $PORT (8080 by default) with plain HTTP, and keep instances stateless.

A question about deploying a function from source is testing `gcloud run deploy --source . --function ENTRYPOINT --base-image`, and a public service blocked by Domain restricted sharing is testing --no-invoker-iam-check.

A question that reacts to uploads is testing an Eventarc trigger on object.v1.finalized in the bucket's location with the Storage service agent allowed to publish; Pub/Sub to a private service needs a push subscription with an invoker service account.

quiz.q: A Cloud Run service receives messages through a Pub/Sub push subscription. When it gets a message with a malformed payload, it logs the problem and returns HTTP 500. The team notices the same malformed message arriving again and again. What explains this, and what should the service do?
choices: Push subscriptions resend every message once per hour, so the service should store message IDs and ignore the repeats
The invoker service account lacks roles/run.invoker, so Pub/Sub retries; grant the role to stop the repeated deliveries
An error code makes Pub/Sub retry delivery; return a success code such as 204 for messages the service decides to drop
The topic has message ordering on, so Pub/Sub blocks later messages; disable ordering to stop the repeated delivery
quiz.explain: The HTTP response is the acknowledgement: success codes ack the message and error codes make Pub/Sub retry it. Choice B is tempting because missing invoker rights also cause retries, but then the service would never run, and here it is running and returning 500 itself.

quiz.q: A developer deploys a Cloud Run function with gcloud run deploy orders --source . --function handler --base-image BASE_IMAGE. The code in main.py defines a single function named process_order. Deployment fails because the function cannot be found. What should the developer change?
choices: Set --function to process_order, because the flag names the entry point function in the code
Rename main.py to handler.py, because the --function flag names the source file that contains the entry point
Replace --source with --image, because Cloud Run functions must be built as images before gcloud run deploy
Add --allow-unauthenticated, because a function cannot be located until its service accepts anonymous callers
quiz.explain: The --function flag is the entry point: the function name in the code, here process_order. Choice B is tempting because file names matter to some runtimes, but the flag names the function, not the file.

days.recap: Deploy Cloud Run services from an image or with --source, honor the container contract, deploy functions with --function and --base-image, make services public with --no-invoker-iam-check, deliver Pub/Sub messages through authenticated push or Eventarc, and react to Cloud Storage uploads with an object.v1.finalized trigger in the bucket's location.

days.title: Choosing Data Products: Databases, Analytics, Caching and Messaging
services: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka

concepts.heading: Relational Options: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner
concepts.body: Three managed services speak SQL, and the exam separates them by how they scale. Cloud SQL is fully managed MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server. Google runs the VM, storage, backups, patching and maintenance, and the high availability option adds a standby in another zone with automatic failover. Pick it for lift and shift when the goal is the same engine with less administration. AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a PostgreSQL-compatible engine built by Google for demanding work. A columnar engine speeds up analytical queries and read pool instances add load-balanced read nodes, so reports can run on live transactional data (HTAP) instead of a copy loaded every night. Both Cloud SQL and AlloyDB send every write to one primary: they scale reads, not writes. Spanner shards data automatically and scales reads and writes horizontally while keeping transactions strongly consistent, with single-region, dual-region or multi-region configurations. Global orders that must never double-sell a seat point to Spanner.

concepts.heading: NoSQL Options: Firestore and Bigtable
concepts.body: Firestore is a serverless document database. Records are documents with fields, nested maps and arrays, grouped in collections, close to the JSON objects an app holds in memory. There is nothing to provision: it scales compute and storage with the load and charges per use. It offers strongly consistent queries, transactions, multi-region replication and Firebase integration, so mobile and web apps talk to it through the Firebase SDKs; a MongoDB-compatible API also exists. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL database for very large amounts of single-keyed data with low latency and high read and write throughput: time series, IoT readings, financial ticks and marketing events. Its only index is the row key and rows are stored sorted by it, so a key such as sensor42#20261030T0815 turns one device's hour into a fast range scan. Throughput grows with the number of nodes, clusters resize without downtime, and an HBase-compatible client eases moves from Apache HBase.

concepts.heading: BigQuery for Analytics and Memorystore for Caching
concepts.body: Operational databases serve applications with many small reads and writes. BigQuery is the data warehouse: a serverless platform where storage and compute are separate and scale independently, so you never size or patch servers. Analysts write SQL (or Python) that scans terabytes in seconds, and BI tools connect through ODBC and JDBC drivers. When a question says ad hoc SQL over large historical data with no infrastructure to manage, the answer is BigQuery, not a bigger Cloud SQL instance. Memorystore sits at the other end: fully managed in-memory stores for sessions, leaderboards and hot rows that would otherwise hit a disk-based database on every request. Memorystore for Redis is Redis-protocol compliant, so applications that already use an open source Redis client move without code changes. Instances are reached on private IP addresses from an authorized VPC network, and the Standard Tier replicates across zones with automatic failover. Memorystore for Valkey and for Memcached are other engines in the family.

concepts.heading: Messaging: Pub/Sub or Managed Service for Apache Kafka
concepts.body: Pub/Sub is Google's serverless, asynchronous messaging service. Publishers send messages to a topic and move on; subscribers receive them through subscriptions, so producers and consumers are decoupled and can scale on their own. It uses its own API with per-message leasing rather than Kafka partitions, and there is no cluster to size. Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs real open source Apache Kafka for you. You choose the total vCPU and memory of a cluster, and the service provisions brokers, patches them and manages storage. Clients reach private bootstrap addresses in your VPC networks and authenticate with IAM principals over SASL or with mTLS. The decision is about existing code. Producers, consumers and tools that already speak the Kafka API keep working unchanged on the managed Kafka service. A new event-driven design with no Kafka history is usually simpler on Pub/Sub, which needs no capacity planning at all.

concepts.heading: Dataflow and the Streaming Pipeline
concepts.body: Dataflow is the fully managed runner for Apache Beam pipelines. One programming model covers batch and streaming: the same pipeline can read a day of files or an endless stream of events. Dataflow provisions and autoscales its worker VMs, processes each record exactly once by default, and writes to sinks such as BigQuery, Cloud Storage or Bigtable. The pattern to recognize is Pub/Sub, then Dataflow, then BigQuery. Devices or game servers publish events to a topic, a streaming Dataflow job reads the subscription, cleans and enriches records, computes per-minute windows, and appends the results to a BigQuery table that analysts query with SQL. Pub/Sub alone only moves messages and BigQuery alone only stores and queries, so transformation in flight is the clue for Dataflow. For quick sorting practice: Cloud SQL equals same engine, AlloyDB equals PostgreSQL plus analytics, Spanner equals global writes, Firestore equals app documents, Bigtable equals keyed time series, BigQuery equals warehouse, Memorystore equals cache.

examPoints: A question that needs relational SQL plus strongly consistent writes that scale across regions is testing Spanner, because Cloud SQL and AlloyDB scale reads with replicas but keep one primary for writes.
A question about huge volumes of time-stamped device data read by key with low latency, or an HBase workload, is testing Bigtable rather than BigQuery or Firestore.
A question in which applications already use Kafka clients and tools is testing Managed Service for Apache Kafka, while new decoupled event services with no cluster to size point to Pub/Sub.

quiz.q: A web shop reads the same product rows thousands of times a minute from Cloud SQL, and the primary's CPU stays high. The developers already use an open source Redis client library. What should the team add?
choices: A Bigtable instance in front of Cloud SQL, with the product rows copied in nightly and read by row key
A Memorystore for Redis instance in the same VPC network, used as a cache for the hot product rows
An AlloyDB read pool for the catalog, after migrating the whole database from Cloud SQL to AlloyDB
A Firestore database for the product rows, with Firebase SDKs replacing the Redis client in the app
quiz.explain: Memorystore for Redis is a managed in-memory cache that is Redis-protocol compliant, so the existing client works and the primary stops serving every read. Choice C also offloads reads, but it means a database migration when the stated need is a cache for code that already speaks Redis.

quiz.q: Clickstream events arrive from many websites. Before landing in BigQuery they must be cleaned, joined with a product list and aggregated every minute, and the team wants workers that scale themselves. Which design fits?
choices: Publish events to Pub/Sub and use a BigQuery subscription that writes the raw messages straight to a table
Write events to Cloud SQL and run a scheduled query every minute that copies new rows into BigQuery
Send events to Memorystore and have a Cloud Run job read the cache every minute and load it into BigQuery
Publish events to Pub/Sub and run a streaming Dataflow pipeline that transforms and writes them to BigQuery
quiz.explain: Dataflow runs Apache Beam streaming pipelines with autoscaled workers, so cleaning, joining and windowed aggregation happen in flight between Pub/Sub and BigQuery. Choice A delivers messages, but it only lands raw data and does no transformation or aggregation on the way.

days.recap: Cloud SQL keeps the engine, AlloyDB adds PostgreSQL analytics, Spanner scales global consistent writes, Firestore serves app documents, Bigtable handles keyed time series, BigQuery is the warehouse, Memorystore caches, Pub/Sub or managed Kafka moves events, and Dataflow transforms them.

days.title: Storage Products, Storage Classes, Loading Data and Bucket Locations

concepts.heading: Block, File and Object Storage
concepts.body: Start from how the data is used. Block storage, meaning Persistent Disk and Google Cloud Hyperdisk, is a disk attached to a VM, and its options for many writers at once are limited. Object storage is Cloud Storage: whole objects reached through an API or gcloud storage, with practically unlimited capacity. Cloud Storage FUSE can mount a bucket like a folder, but it lacks some file-system behavior. File storage is a shared file system. Filestore is a managed NFS file server that Compute Engine VMs, GKE clusters, Cloud Run services and on-premises machines mount over NFSv3 (all tiers) or NFSv4.1. Many clients can read and write at the same time, so GKE PersistentVolumes can be mounted read-write by many nodes, and unlike FUSE it offers POSIX compliance, hard links and file locking. When a scenario says that many VMs or Pods share one read-write directory, think Filestore; when it says that one VM needs a fast boot or data disk, think Hyperdisk or Persistent Disk.

concepts.heading: NetApp Volumes and Managed Lustre
concepts.body: Two more file services fill gaps that Filestore leaves. Google Cloud NetApp Volumes is fully managed file and block storage with NFSv3, NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.2, SMB and iSCSI, plus automated snapshots, backups, auto-tiering and volume replication. Protocol is the quickest filter: Windows file shares mapped as network drives use SMB, and Filestore offers no SMB, so a Windows share or a mix of SMB and NFS from one service points to NetApp Volumes. It also helps move enterprise workloads without re-architecting them. Managed Lustre is a fully managed parallel file system for AI and HPC, built with DDN. A single file server becomes a bottleneck when hundreds of training or simulation nodes read the same data at once; a parallel file system spreads files across many storage servers, so throughput grows with the system. Managed Lustre is POSIX compliant, integrates with Compute Engine and GKE, scales to multiple petabytes, and offers fast managed transfers into and out of Cloud Storage.

concepts.heading: Five Storage Classes
concepts.body: Every Cloud Storage object has a storage class, and a bucket's default class is only what new objects get when the upload names none. Standard is for hot data, with no minimum storage duration and no retrieval fees. Nearline suits access about once a month, with a 30-day minimum. Coldline suits access about once a quarter, with a 90-day minimum. Archive suits access less than once a year, with a 365-day minimum, yet it still returns data in milliseconds with no thaw step. Nearline, Coldline and Archive charge retrieval fees, and deleting or rewriting early bills the rest of the minimum. These four work in regions, dual-regions and multi-regions. The fifth class, Rapid storage, is different: it exists only in zonal buckets created through Rapid Bucket, places data in the same zone as your compute, and targets I/O-intensive AI, ML and analytics work with very low latency, not lower storage cost. It has no minimum duration and no retrieval fees. Changing a bucket's default class never changes existing objects.

concepts.heading: Loading Data into Cloud Storage and BigQuery
concepts.body: Google's guidance picks the tool by size and source. Under 1 TB from a workstation or on-premises server, use gcloud storage: `gcloud storage cp --recursive ./media gs://BUCKET` copies a folder tree, `--storage-class=NEARLINE` sets the class of the new objects, and `--no-clobber` skips files that already exist. For more than 1 TB on-premises, use Storage Transfer Service with agents, or Transfer Appliance when the network is poor. For data in Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, another bucket or HTTP URLs, use Storage Transfer Service: scheduled, parallel jobs with retries and integrity checks. Into BigQuery, `bq load` reads one URI, a list or a wildcard such as gs://bucket/2026/*.csv. The bucket must be in the same location as the dataset, or the job fails. `--skip_leading_rows=1` drops a CSV header, `--autodetect` infers the schema, appending is the default, and `--replace` truncates the table first, dropping its old data and schema.

concepts.heading: Bucket Locations and Redundancy
concepts.body: A bucket's location type decides how it survives an outage. A region keeps data redundant across zones in one region and is the lowest-cost location, but a regional outage affects it. A dual-region is a specific pair of regions, either a predefined pair or a configurable pair chosen with `--placement`. A multi-region is a large area such as US, EU or ASIA, where Google chooses the data centers. Dual-regions and multi-regions are active-active: during a regional outage the same bucket keeps serving under the same name, so applications need no change. Replication between regions is asynchronous. Default replication targets 99.9 percent of new objects within one hour and all of them within 12 hours. Turbo replication targets all new objects within 15 minutes, is available only for dual-region buckets, and is set with `--rpo=ASYNC_TURBO` on `gcloud storage buckets create` or update. A requirement that names two specific regions and a 15-minute recovery point therefore points to a dual-region bucket with turbo replication, not a multi-region.

examPoints: A question that asks for Windows SMB shares, or SMB and NFS from one managed service, is testing NetApp Volumes, because Filestore serves NFS only.
A question that matches an access frequency to a class is testing Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days and Archive 365 days, with Rapid storage reserved for zonal, high-performance buckets.
A question about a BigQuery load from Cloud Storage that fails at once is often testing the rule that the bucket and the dataset must be in the same location.

quiz.q: A GPU training cluster in one zone of us-central1 reads millions of small objects per epoch, and storage latency keeps the GPUs idle. The data can be rebuilt from a source bucket if the zone fails. Which storage choice fits?
choices: An Archive class bucket in the US multi-region, so the objects are stored redundantly across several regions
A Standard class dual-region bucket with turbo replication, so new objects reach the second region quickly
A zonal bucket with Rapid storage in the same zone as the GPUs, so reads stay close to the compute nodes
A Nearline class regional bucket in us-central1, so the objects live in the same region as the GPU nodes
quiz.explain: Rapid storage lives in zonal buckets colocated with compute and is built for I/O-intensive AI and analytics work, and the data can be rebuilt, so zonal placement is acceptable. Choice B improves recovery point, not read latency, and dual-region data is not placed next to the GPUs.

quiz.q: Every night a job loads a full export of the customer list from gs://crm-exports/customers.csv into the BigQuery table crm.customers. Each night's file must completely replace the previous night's rows. Which load flag gives that result?
choices: `--replace`, which truncates the table before writing the new rows from the CSV file
`--noreplace`, which appends the new rows after the rows already stored in the table
