`--autodetect`, which infers the schema and replaces rows whose key matches the CSV
`--skip_leading_rows=1`, which skips the old rows and writes only the new CSV rows
quiz.explain: `--replace` (WRITE_TRUNCATE) erases the table's existing data before the load, so the table holds only the newest export. Choice B is the default append behavior, which would pile up duplicates every night.

days.recap: Pick block, file or object storage by access pattern, use NetApp Volumes for SMB and Managed Lustre for parallel AI and HPC, match classes to access frequency with Rapid for zonal speed, load with gcloud storage, Storage Transfer Service or bq load, and choose dual-region with turbo for a short recovery point.

days.title: VPC Networks, Firewalls, Hybrid Connectivity and Load Balancers

concepts.heading: Custom Mode VPC Networks and Subnets
concepts.body: A VPC network is a global resource: one network, with its routes and firewall rules, can hold subnets in many regions. Each subnet is regional and has its own primary IPv4 range, usable by VMs in any zone of that region. An auto mode network, like the default network of a new project, gets one subnet in every region from ranges inside 10.128.0.0/9 and grows automatically when regions launch. A custom mode network starts empty, and you pick every region and range yourself, which is why Google recommends it for production. You can convert auto mode to custom mode, but not back. A typical build is `gcloud compute networks create prod-net --subnet-mode=custom` followed by `gcloud compute networks subnets create prod-usc1 --network=prod-net --range=10.20.0.0/20 --region=us-central1`. A subnet's primary range can be expanded later without downtime, but never shrunk.

concepts.heading: Shared VPC and VPC Network Peering
concepts.body: Shared VPC lets one host project own a network while service projects in the same organization run resources in its subnets. A Shared VPC Admin enables the host and attaches service projects. Service project admins receive Compute Network User (`roles/compute.networkUser`) on the whole host project or only on chosen subnets, so they create VMs in their own project, billed there, without changing the network, while network and security admins in the host project manage subnets and firewall rules. Attaching a project changes nothing that already exists; new resources must choose a shared subnet. VPC Network Peering instead joins two separate networks, in the same or different projects or even organizations, so they talk over internal IP addresses. Each side must create a peering that names the other before the state becomes ACTIVE. Subnet ranges may not overlap, routing is not transitive (A to B and B to C does not connect A to C), and firewall rules are never shared, so each side still writes its own ingress rules.

concepts.heading: VPC Firewall Rules and Cloud NGFW Policies
concepts.body: When no rule matches, Cloud NGFW ends with an implied action: deny for ingress to VM interfaces, allow for egress. You add rules with an action, direction, priority, source or destination, protocols and ports, and targets. The lowest priority number wins, and deny beats allow only at equal priority. Targets can be all instances, network tags or service accounts. Network tags are free-form strings that anyone who can edit a VM can change, while a VM's service account changes only when the VM is stopped and attaching it requires IAM permission, so service accounts give stricter control. Cloud NGFW firewall policies group rules above or beside the network. Hierarchical firewall policies attach to the organization or a folder, are evaluated first, and use allow, deny or goto_next; lower levels cannot override them. Global and regional network firewall policies attach to networks in a project. Policies can use secure tags: IAM-governed tag values with purpose GCE_FIREWALL, created by a Tag Administrator and bound to VMs by principals with Tag User, so teams choose which rules apply without editing the rules.

concepts.heading: Cloud VPN Versus Cloud Interconnect
concepts.body: Hybrid connectivity questions turn on bandwidth, speed of setup and encryption. Cloud VPN builds IPsec tunnels over the internet, so traffic is encrypted and the link can be ready in hours on an ordinary internet line. HA VPN gateways have two interfaces with their own external addresses; with tunnels on both, in a supported topology, they offer a 99.99 percent SLA, and Cloud Router exchanges routes with BGP. It suits modest bandwidth, lower cost and migration experiments. Cloud Interconnect keeps traffic off the public internet. Dedicated Interconnect is a direct physical link in a supported colocation facility, in 10-Gbps, 100-Gbps or 400-Gbps circuits, and you must install your own routing equipment there. Partner Interconnect reaches Google through a service provider, with VLAN attachments from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps and no equipment of yours in a colocation facility. Interconnect is not IPsec-encrypted by itself; when policy demands encryption you can run HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect.

concepts.heading: Choosing Load Balancers and Network Service Tiers
concepts.body: Start from the traffic type. Application Load Balancers handle HTTP and HTTPS as proxies, with URL maps that route by host or path. Proxy Network Load Balancers handle TCP. Passthrough Network Load Balancers handle TCP, UDP and other IP protocols without terminating connections, so backends see the original client address and reply directly. Next choose external for internet clients or internal for clients in the VPC network and networks connected to it, then global or regional by where backends live. Network Service Tiers decide how internet traffic travels. Premium Tier, the default, enters and leaves Google's backbone close to users and supports global external IP addresses. Standard Tier costs less, enters and leaves near the resource's region, and supports regional resources only. Set it per resource or as a project default with `gcloud compute project-info update --default-network-tier=STANDARD`.

examPoints: A question about several departments deploying into one centrally managed network is testing Shared VPC, with Compute Network User granted on specific subnets to limit each team.
A question in which two peered spokes still cannot reach each other is testing that VPC Network Peering is non-transitive and never shares firewall rules.

A question that lists traffic type, client location and the need to keep client IP addresses is testing load balancer choice: HTTP(S) means Application Load Balancer, UDP or client IP preservation means passthrough.

quiz.q: An internal HTTP API runs on VMs in one region. Only clients inside the same VPC network may call it, and requests for /reports must go to a separate backend from requests for /orders. Which load balancer fits?
choices: An external passthrough Network Load Balancer with a forwarding rule for each URL path of the API
An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer with one backend service that serves both URL paths
A global external Application Load Balancer with a URL map and a firewall rule that blocks the internet
A regional internal Application Load Balancer with a URL map that routes each path to its own backend
quiz.explain: A regional internal Application Load Balancer serves clients inside the VPC network and uses a URL map to route by path. Choice B is internal, but a passthrough load balancer forwards packets without reading HTTP, so it cannot send /reports and /orders to different backends.

quiz.q: A team runs a regional VM that serves large file downloads to internet users. It needs no global load balancing, and the team accepts traffic leaving Google's network near the VM's region in exchange for lower networking cost. What should the team configure?
choices: Premium Tier for the VM's external IP address, because Premium is the lower-cost tier for single-region traffic
Standard Tier for the VM's external IP address, because Standard Tier routes traffic near the region for less cost
Cloud Interconnect between the VM and its users, because private links lower the cost of internet downloads
A global external Application Load Balancer in Standard Tier, because global load balancers support both tiers
quiz.explain: Standard Tier enters and leaves Google's network near the region of the IP address and costs less, which suits a regional VM. Choice D is wrong because global external load balancers need global IP addresses, which exist only in Premium Tier.

days.recap: Build custom mode VPC networks with planned regional subnets, share them with Shared VPC or connect them with non-transitive peering, write firewall rules and Cloud NGFW policies with service accounts or secure tags, pick HA VPN or Interconnect by bandwidth, and choose load balancers by traffic type and scope.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code and AI-Assisted Planning Tools

concepts.heading: Terraform and Remote State
concepts.body: Terraform describes the desired end state of your infrastructure in HCL configuration files. `terraform plan` shows what would change and `terraform apply` calls the Google Cloud APIs, then records the result in a state file that maps each resource in the configuration to a real resource. On the next run Terraform compares configuration, state and reality to decide what to create, update or destroy. By default state is a local terraform.tfstate file, which breaks teamwork: each laptop has its own picture of what exists, so one engineer's apply can try to recreate what another already built. Google's docs store shared state in a Cloud Storage bucket through the gcs backend, with a block such as backend gcs naming the bucket and a prefix per environment. Turn on Object Versioning on that bucket so earlier state versions can be recovered, then run `terraform init` to move the local state into it. Terraform modules package reusable building blocks, such as a standard VPC network with its subnets.

concepts.heading: Infrastructure Manager and the End of Deployment Manager
concepts.body: Infrastructure Manager (Infra Manager) is Google's managed service for running Terraform. You point it at a Terraform configuration, called a blueprint, stored in a Cloud Storage bucket, a Git repository or a local directory, and create a deployment. Infra Manager starts a Cloud Build job on a Google-maintained image that runs terraform init, validate and apply, streams logs to a bucket and keeps the state for you. Each update is a revision that records its logs, configuration, resource list and state file, and preview deployments show what a change would do before you apply it. Infra Manager manages infrastructure, not application rollout; tools such as Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy handle that. Cloud Deployment Manager reached end of support on March 31, 2026. Existing resources it created keep working and can be managed with normal tools, but new users are blocked, and Google directs customers to Infrastructure Manager or another tool. On the exam, Deployment Manager is never the right answer for new work.

concepts.heading: Config Connector: Google Cloud Resources as Kubernetes Objects
concepts.body: Config Connector is an open source Kubernetes add-on that installs custom resource definitions and controllers in a cluster. You write a manifest such as a StorageBucket or PubSubTopic, apply it with kubectl or a GitOps tool, and the controller creates the Google Cloud resource and keeps reconciling it to the declared state. If someone changes the resource by hand, the controller drifts it back. Reconciliation runs with the Config Connector service account's identity, not with the identity of the person who applied the manifest, so access is governed by who may change the repository and by the roles of that service account. The appeal is one workflow and one source of truth: teams that already deploy applications as Kubernetes YAML can declare the database, bucket and topic their app needs next to the Deployment. Compare it with Terraform, which uses HCL and its own plan and apply cycle with state, and with Helm, which installs Kubernetes objects but does not call Google Cloud APIs by itself.

concepts.heading: Helm Charts in Artifact Registry
concepts.body: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart bundles templated manifests such as Deployments, Services and ConfigMaps with default values; `helm install` or `helm upgrade` renders them with per-environment values and applies them to a cluster, and versioned charts make rollbacks simple. To keep charts private on Google Cloud, store them in Artifact Registry. There is no separate Helm repository format: Artifact Registry stores Helm 3 charts as OCI artifacts in Docker-format repositories. Helm authenticates to Artifact Registry and pushes with `helm push` to an oci:// address, and clusters install from that address. Access is controlled with Artifact Registry IAM roles such as Artifact Registry Reader. Container Registry shut down on March 18, 2025, so new images and charts belong in Artifact Registry, never in gcr.io.

concepts.heading: Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist and Application Design Center
concepts.body: Three AI-assisted tools help plan and build, and the exam separates them by where they work. Gemini CLI is an open source AI agent in your terminal, available in Cloud Shell without setup. It reasons and acts with built-in tools that read and edit local files and run shell commands, and it can call MCP servers, so it can draft a Terraform module and run terraform plan in the same session. Gemini Cloud Assist is the assistant in the Google Cloud console. It answers questions with your project's context, generates gcloud commands, Kubernetes manifests and Terraform, and runs investigations that troubleshoot issues from logs and metrics. Application Design Center lets platform teams publish governed application templates built from Google components or their own Terraform modules, share them through catalogs, and check them against Security Command Center frameworks with a security scorecard before deployment. Developers start from a template on a visual canvas, through chat with Gemini Cloud Assist, the API or gcloud. Agent Runtime, by contrast, hosts your own agents.

examPoints: A question about several engineers whose Terraform runs conflict is testing remote state in a Cloud Storage bucket through the gcs backend, with Object Versioning on.
A question that offers Cloud Deployment Manager for new infrastructure is testing that it reached end of support on March 31, 2026; choose Infrastructure Manager or Terraform.
A question that asks where to keep private Helm charts is testing that Artifact Registry stores them as OCI artifacts in a Docker-format repository.

quiz.q: A team still keeps old Deployment Manager templates and wants new environments described in Terraform, run by a managed Google Cloud service that keeps the state and records each change as a revision. What should the team use?
choices: Infrastructure Manager, deploying Terraform configurations stored in a Git repository or a Cloud Storage bucket
Cloud Deployment Manager, converting each Terraform module into a Jinja template that it can deploy and track
Config Connector, applying the Terraform files to a GKE cluster that turns them into Kubernetes resources
Gemini Cloud Assist, running the Terraform files from the console chat and storing state in the conversation
quiz.explain: Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform as a managed service, keeps state and stores each update as a revision. Choice B is wrong because Deployment Manager reached end of support on March 31, 2026 and is not offered to new users.

quiz.q: A platform team wants to keep its Helm charts private on Google Cloud, next to the container images that the charts deploy, and install them into GKE with helm. Where should the charts go?
choices: A Cloud Storage bucket with public access prevention, served to helm through a signed URL for every chart
A Container Registry host such as gcr.io, which stores Helm charts beside the images in the same project
An Artifact Registry Docker-format repository, where helm push stores each chart as an OCI artifact
An Artifact Registry repository created in a separate Helm format, which serves charts through index files
quiz.explain: Artifact Registry stores Helm 3 charts as OCI artifacts in Docker-format repositories, reached with oci:// addresses. Choice D sounds right, but Artifact Registry has no separate Helm repository format, and Choice B is a registry that shut down in March 2025.

days.recap: Keep Terraform state in a versioned Cloud Storage bucket, let Infrastructure Manager run Terraform now that Deployment Manager is past end of support, use Config Connector for Kubernetes-style resources, store Helm charts as OCI artifacts, and match Gemini CLI, Cloud Assist and Application Design Center to terminal, console and templates.

days.title: Managing Compute Engine Instances, Accelerators and AI Workspaces

concepts.heading: SSH and IAP TCP Forwarding
concepts.body: The usual way into a Linux VM is `gcloud compute ssh VM`, which handles keys for you. A VM without an external IP address can still be reached through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding: IAP proxies carry an encrypted tunnel from your workstation to the VM's internal address. Two separate checks must pass. On the network side, a VPC firewall rule must allow ingress from the IAP range 35.235.240.0/20 on the forwarded port, such as TCP 22 for SSH or 3389 for RDP. On the identity side, the user needs the IAP-secured Tunnel User role (`roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`) on the project or on one VM, and IAM Conditions can narrow it further. For SSH, add `--tunnel-through-iap` to gcloud compute ssh. For any other port, run `gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel VM 3389 --local-host-port=localhost:3389` and point the client at the local port. The VM keeps no public address, and every connection is checked against IAM.

concepts.heading: Listing and Inspecting Instances
concepts.body: Inventory work is done with list and describe commands. `gcloud compute instances list` shows VMs in all zones of the project by default, and `--zones` narrows the output. Every list command accepts `--filter`, a Boolean expression checked per resource. A VM's status field holds values such as RUNNING, STOPPING and TERMINATED, and a stopped VM shows TERMINATED, so `--filter=status=RUNNING` lists only running VMs and a name expression like `name~^web-` matches by regular expression. `--format` and `--sort-by` shape the output, for example a table of name, zone and status to paste into a ticket. `gcloud compute instances describe VM --zone=ZONE` is the opposite: every field of one VM, including its service account, disks, metadata and scheduling policy. In the console the VM instances page shows the same list with filters. For an inventory across many projects or the whole organization, Cloud Asset Inventory searches every resource type at once.

concepts.heading: Snapshots, Snapshot Schedules and Images
concepts.body: Several resources save VM state, and the exam tests which fits. A standard snapshot backs up one disk, incrementally and geo-redundantly. A snapshot schedule is a regional resource policy that takes standard snapshots hourly, daily or weekly; create it with `gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule` and attach it with `gcloud compute disks add-resource-policies`. Its retention applies only to snapshots it created, and an old snapshot is deleted only when a newer one of that disk exists. When the source disk is deleted, scheduled snapshots are kept by default unless the deletion rule applies the retention policy. A custom image is a bootable copy of one disk used to create many VMs, often grouped in an image family; deprecating the newest image rolls the family back to the previous one. An instance template holds configuration only, without disk data. A machine image captures a whole VM, with configuration, metadata, permissions and the data of all its disks, which suits cloning or backing up a multi-disk VM.

concepts.heading: Attaching GPUs and Using TPUs
concepts.body: GPUs on Compute Engine come in two ways. Accelerator-optimized machine types, the A-series and G-series, have GPUs built in, and you change the count by moving to another machine type in the same series. N1 general-purpose machine types, except shared-core ones, can have GPUs such as nvidia-tesla-t4 attached. To add a GPU to an existing N1 VM, stop it, set the host maintenance policy to TERMINATE because GPU VMs cannot live migrate, add the GPU type and count, start the VM and install a GPU driver. GPUs and TPUs exist only in certain zones, so check zone availability first. In GKE, GPU nodes added beside CPU node pools are tainted, and a Pod that requests nvidia.com/gpu in its limits receives the matching toleration automatically. Tensor Processing Units are Google's custom ASICs for large matrix operations, compiled through XLA. You use them through Compute Engine, GKE or Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; the older Cloud TPU API is deprecated.

concepts.heading: Workstations, Notebooks and Agent Runtime
concepts.body: Cloud Workstations gives developers managed environments. A workstation cluster sets the region and VPC network, a workstation configuration is the template (machine type, container image with the tools and IDE, persistent storage, timeouts and access), and each workstation is one developer's instance. Workstations run on ephemeral VMs; only the persistent home directory survives a stop, and configuration changes apply at the next start. For data science, Agent Platform Workbench (formerly Vertex AI Workbench) instances are JupyterLab VMs you own, with optional GPUs and an idle shutdown. Its executor runs a notebook once or on a schedule on custom training, even while the instance is off, and saves results in Cloud Storage. Colab Enterprise notebooks in BigQuery Studio mix SQL and Python cells with no VM to manage. Agent Runtime (formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine) deploys and scales your own AI agents: Python agents from source files, a linked Git repository or the SDK, and any-language agents from a Dockerfile or an Artifact Registry container image.

examPoints: A question about reaching a VM that has no external IP address is testing IAP TCP forwarding: a firewall rule from 35.235.240.0/20 plus the IAP-secured Tunnel User role.
A question that compares a snapshot, a custom image, an instance template and a machine image is testing what each captures: one disk, a boot image, configuration only, or the whole VM.
A question about adding a GPU to an N1 VM is testing the steps: stop the VM, set host maintenance to TERMINATE, add the GPU, start it and install the driver.

quiz.q: An operator must hand a manager the names of every stopped VM in the project, across all zones. Which command produces that list?
choices: `gcloud compute instances describe --filter=status=STOPPED`, which prints the stopped VMs with all their fields
`gcloud compute instances list --filter=status=TERMINATED`, which lists every zone and keeps only stopped VMs
`gcloud compute instances list --zones=all --status=stopped`, which limits the output to VMs that are stopped
`gcloud compute instances list --filter=status=RUNNING`, which lists the running VMs so the rest are stopped
quiz.explain: instances list covers all zones by default, and a stopped VM has the status TERMINATED, so filtering on that value returns exactly the stopped VMs. Choice A uses describe, which shows one named VM, and STOPPED is not the status value a stopped VM reports.

quiz.q: A data disk on a reporting VM needs a backup every day at 01:00, and backups older than 30 days should be removed automatically. Which approach fits?
choices: Create a machine image of the VM every day with a cron job, and delete machine images by hand each month
Create a custom image from the data disk every day and add each image to an image family for the reports
Create an instance template that includes the data disk, so the template keeps a daily copy of the disk data
Attach a snapshot schedule to the disk with a daily 01:00 snapshot and 30 days of retention
quiz.explain: A snapshot schedule takes standard snapshots of the disk on a timetable and deletes scheduled snapshots after the retention period. Choice C is wrong because an instance template stores only configuration, never the data on the disks.

days.recap: Reach private VMs through IAP with the 35.235.240.0/20 firewall rule and Tunnel User role, list instances with filters, back up disks with snapshot schedules and whole VMs with machine images, stop N1 VMs to attach GPUs, and use Workstations, Workbench, BigQuery notebooks and Agent Runtime for developer and AI work.

days.title: Operating GKE Workloads and Cloud Run Services

concepts.heading: Node Pools and the Cluster Autoscaler
concepts.body: A GKE Standard cluster runs workloads on node pools: groups of nodes with the same machine type, disk and settings. Manage them with gcloud container, for example `gcloud container node-pools create`, update and delete, and look at Kubernetes objects with kubectl. Changing a pool's machine type or boot disk recreates its nodes using the pool's upgrade strategy, surge or blue-green, so Pods are evicted and rescheduled. Deleting a pool removes its nodes, and by default GKE does not respect PodDisruptionBudgets during that deletion unless the pool has `--respect-pdb-during-node-pool-deletion`. The cluster autoscaler adds or removes nodes between a pool's limits. `--min-nodes` and `--max-nodes` count per zone, while `--total-min-nodes` and `--total-max-nodes` count across all zones of the pool. It decides on resource requests, not CPU usage: it scales up when Pods are Pending because no node has room for their requests, and scales down when nodes are underused. Never enable Compute Engine autoscaling on the pool's managed instance group.

concepts.heading: Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscaling
concepts.body: The horizontal Pod autoscaler (HPA) changes the number of replicas of a Deployment or StatefulSet to keep a metric near a target, for example `kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=60 --min=2 --max=10`. A percentage target is usage divided by the container's CPU request, so a percentage target works only when the containers set CPU requests. When new replicas do not fit, they wait as Pending and the cluster autoscaler adds nodes, which is how the two work together. The vertical Pod autoscaler (VPA) studies past usage and recommends CPU and memory requests. Its updateMode decides what happens: Off only records recommendations, Initial sets requests when Pods are created, Auto (Recreate) evicts Pods to apply new values, and InPlaceOrRecreate tries to resize Pods in place first. GKE's docs say not to combine an HPA and a standard VPA on CPU or memory, because changing requests moves the HPA's percentage; pair a VPA with an HPA on custom or external metrics, or use multidimensional Pod autoscaling.

concepts.heading: Autopilot Requests and Pulling from Artifact Registry
concepts.body: In Autopilot, Google manages the nodes, and the resource requests in your Pod spec decide what capacity is provisioned and, with Pod-based billing, what you pay for. Autopilot checks requests against the chosen compute class. With no requests it applies defaults; for the general-purpose class that is 0.5 vCPU, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of ephemeral storage. Requests below the minimum are raised, requests above the maximum are rejected with an error, and a CPU to memory ratio out of range is fixed by raising the smaller resource. If you set only limits, requests are set equal to them. Container images come from Artifact Registry, and the node pulls them with the node's service account, by default the Compute Engine default service account. In the same project, grant that account Artifact Registry Reader (`roles/artifactregistry.reader`). When images live in another project, grant the role on that project or on the repository there; roles in the cluster's own project do not reach it. Image pull errors show in `kubectl describe pod`.

concepts.heading: Pods, Services and StatefulSets
concepts.body: A Pod is one or more containers that share a network address; you rarely create Pods directly. A Deployment manages interchangeable replicas with random names, ideal for stateless web and API servers. A StatefulSet gives each replica a stable identity: ordinal names such as db-0 and db-1, a stable hostname, and its own PersistentVolumeClaim created from volumeClaimTemplates, which follows the Pod when it is rescheduled. Pair it with a headless Service so each replica gets a DNS name such as db-0.db.default.svc.cluster.local. Pod IP addresses change when Pods move, so clients use Services. A ClusterIP Service, the default, gives a stable internal address reachable inside the cluster. NodePort extends it by opening a port on each node. LoadBalancer extends NodePort and has GKE create a network load balancer with an address that clients outside the cluster can use. For checks, `kubectl get pods -o wide` adds each Pod's IP and node, and `kubectl get services` shows type, cluster IP and external IP.

concepts.heading: Cloud Run Revisions, Traffic Splitting and Autoscaling
concepts.body: Every Cloud Run deployment creates an immutable revision, and the service's traffic settings say which revisions receive what share. `gcloud run deploy SERVICE --image IMAGE --no-traffic --tag canary` creates a revision with no traffic but its own URL, such as https://canary---SERVICE-HASH.a.run.app, for testing. `gcloud run services update-traffic SERVICE --to-tags canary=10` or `--to-revisions REV=PERCENT` shifts traffic gradually, and setting the share back rolls back. A new service sends all traffic to the latest revision, but once you pin traffic to a named revision, later deployments receive nothing until you run update-traffic with `--to-latest`. Each revision autoscales on request concurrency and CPU utilization, not on memory, and scales to zero when idle, so the next request waits for a cold start. Minimum instances keep warm instances ready and remove cold starts at the cost of paying while idle. Maximum instances cap scale-out to protect a backing database; beyond the cap, requests wait briefly and may fail with HTTP 429.

examPoints: A question in which nodes never scale out while CPU is high is testing that the cluster autoscaler reacts to Pending Pods and requests, not to usage.
A question about an HPA that shows no CPU percentage is testing that a percentage target needs CPU requests on the containers.
A question in which new Cloud Run revisions get no traffic after a rollback is testing pinned traffic, fixed with update-traffic --to-latest or an explicit share.

quiz.q: A developer deploys a Pod to a GKE Autopilot cluster with a CPU request smaller than the minimum that the general-purpose compute class allows. What does Autopilot do?
choices: It rejects the Pod with an error, because any request outside the allowed range blocks the workload
It keeps the small request and lets the Pod burst onto spare node capacity whenever it needs more CPU
It raises the CPU request to bring it into the allowed range, and then schedules the Pod normally
It ignores the request and applies the default of 0.5 vCPU to every container in the same cluster
quiz.explain: Autopilot raises requests that are below the minimum and only rejects requests that are above the maximum. Choice A mixes up the two limits: rejection is the behavior for requests that are too large.

quiz.q: A Deployment named shop-web runs in a GKE Standard cluster. Customers on the internet must reach it on one stable external address without any extra components such as an Ingress. Which Service type should the team create?
choices: LoadBalancer, which makes GKE create a network load balancer with an external address for the Pods
ClusterIP, which gives the Pods a stable address that clients on the internet can reach directly
A headless Service, which publishes one stable public DNS name for each Pod of the Deployment
NodePort alone, which opens a port on each node and gives the Service a single external address
quiz.explain: A LoadBalancer Service extends NodePort and has GKE create a network load balancer with an address clients outside the cluster can use. Choice D is wrong because NodePort only exposes a port on each node's address and gives no single stable external address.

days.recap: Manage node pools with gcloud container and let the cluster autoscaler follow requests, scale replicas with HPA and size requests with VPA, respect Autopilot request rules, grant node service accounts Artifact Registry Reader, use StatefulSets and Services correctly, and steer Cloud Run with revisions, tags, traffic splits and instance limits.

days.title: Managing Cloud Storage: Access, Lifecycle, Recovery and Cost

concepts.heading: Uniform Bucket-Level Access and Public Access Prevention
concepts.body: Cloud Storage has two permission systems: IAM roles on the project, a bucket or a managed folder, and older access control lists (ACLs) that can grant access object by object. Uniform bucket-level access turns ACLs off for the bucket and all its objects, so access comes only from IAM. Requests to set or read ACLs then fail, and access that came from existing object ACLs or object ownership stops. The old ACLs are kept, so you can turn the setting off again, but only until it has been on for 90 days in a row. Managed folders need uniform bucket-level access and let you grant IAM roles on a prefix, which replaces most per-object ACL uses. Public access prevention blocks exposure through allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers. Set it per bucket (enforced) or through the organization policy constraint storage.publicAccessPrevention on a project, folder or organization. Existing public grants stay in place but are overridden, new ones fail, and signed URLs keep working.

concepts.heading: Signed URLs
concepts.body: A signed URL carries authentication in its query string, so whoever holds it can perform one action, such as GET on one object, until it expires, without a Google account. The bucket stays private. It is signed with the credentials of an account allowed to perform the action, in most cases a service account. The gcloud command is `gcloud storage sign-url gs://BUCKET/OBJECT --duration=2h --impersonate-service-account=SA_EMAIL`. The default lifetime is one hour. Signing through impersonation avoids downloading a service account key, which is the safer choice, but limits the URL to at most 12 hours. Signing with a service account key file allows up to 7 days, the V4 maximum, at the cost of handling a long-lived key, which Google discourages. So when a link must last a few days, the trade-off is key management, and when a few hours are enough, impersonation is the better answer. Signed URLs also allow uploads, such as a PUT URL that lets a partner drop one file into a private bucket.

concepts.heading: Object Lifecycle Management
concepts.body: A lifecycle configuration is a set of rules on a bucket. Each rule has one action and one or more conditions, and Cloud Storage applies the action asynchronously when all of a rule's conditions match. Actions are Delete, SetStorageClass and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload. Common conditions are age in days, matchesPrefix or matchesSuffix, matchesStorageClass, and for versioned buckets isLive, numNewerVersions and daysSinceNoncurrentTime. SetStorageClass only moves objects to colder classes, and when Delete and SetStorageClass match at once, Delete wins. Write the rules in JSON and apply them with `gcloud storage buckets update gs://BUCKET --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json`; changes can take up to 24 hours. A lifecycle class change does not rewrite the object, so it causes no retrieval or early deletion fee, and time spent in the old class counts toward the new minimum. For example, move logs to Coldline at 90 days and delete them at 365. To keep only two noncurrent versions, delete versions where isLive is false and numNewerVersions is 3, because the count includes the live version.

concepts.heading: Soft Delete and Object Versioning
concepts.body: Soft delete protects against mistakes. When an object is deleted or overwritten, or a whole bucket is deleted, it moves into a soft-deleted state for the retention duration and can be restored during that time. Soft delete is on by default for new buckets with a 7-day retention; you can set 7 to 90 days, or 0 to turn it off. Zonal buckets with Rapid storage do not support it. A new duration applies only to objects deleted after the change; objects already soft deleted keep the duration that applied when they were deleted. Soft-deleted objects cannot be read, only listed and restored, and they keep accruing storage charges. `gcloud storage ls --soft-deleted gs://BUCKET/**` lists them and `gcloud storage restore gs://BUCKET/path/**` brings them back as live objects. Object Versioning is a separate feature: overwriting or deleting turns the old data into a noncurrent version that stays readable until lifecycle rules remove it. Soft delete works with or without versioning, and both add storage cost.

concepts.heading: Estimating and Controlling Storage Cost
concepts.body: A Cloud Storage bill has several parts: at-rest storage by class and location, operations (Class A requests such as uploads and listings, Class B requests such as reads), retrieval fees for Nearline, Coldline and Archive, early deletion charges, and network charges for data sent to the internet or other regions and for dual-region and multi-region replication. Minimum storage durations matter most: Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days, and none for Standard or Rapid. Deleting or rewriting an object early bills the remaining days, so data that lives a month belongs in Standard or Nearline, not Coldline. Autoclass manages classes per object: objects start in Standard, move colder when not read, and return to Standard when read, with no retrieval or early deletion fees but a management fee. It suits unknown access patterns. To estimate before building, use the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator with class, location, volume, operations, retrieval and egress; billing export and budgets only help once resources exist.

examPoints: A question in which object ACL grants stopped working after a bucket change is testing uniform bucket-level access, fixed with IAM on the bucket or a managed folder.
A question about temporary access for someone without a Google account is testing signed URLs, with up to 12 hours when signed through impersonation and up to 7 days with a key.
A question about objects deleted by mistake a few days ago is testing soft delete, with a 7-day default retention and restore through gcloud storage restore.

quiz.q: An engineer runs gcloud storage sign-url on a private object with --impersonate-service-account and --duration=3d so that an auditor can download it over a long weekend. The command fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Signed URLs cannot be created for private buckets, so the bucket must first allow reads by allUsers
Public access prevention on the bucket blocks every signed URL, so the engineer must turn it off first
The --duration flag accepts only minutes, so a value written in days is rejected by the CLI at once
Signing through impersonation limits a signed URL to at most 12 hours, so three days is too long
quiz.explain: When a URL is signed through impersonation, the maximum duration is 12 hours; only signing with a key allows up to 7 days. Choice B is a common mix-up: public access prevention blocks allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers grants but leaves signed URLs working.

quiz.q: Auditors require that objects deleted by mistake from the contracts bucket can be recovered for 30 days. Object Versioning is off, and the bucket uses soft delete with its default settings. What should the team change?
choices: Turn on uniform bucket-level access, so deleted objects keep their IAM grants and can be restored for 30 days
Set the bucket's soft delete retention duration to 30 days, within the range of 7 to 90 days that it allows
Add a lifecycle rule with a Delete action and an age of 30 days, so deleted objects wait 30 days before removal
Move the objects to Coldline, because its 90-day minimum storage duration keeps deleted objects restorable
quiz.explain: Soft delete keeps deleted objects restorable for its retention duration, which can be set from 7 to 90 days, so 30 days meets the requirement; the default is only 7 days. Choice D confuses billing with recovery: a minimum storage duration only adds an early deletion charge and does not keep data restorable.

days.recap: Use uniform bucket-level access and public access prevention for IAM-only private buckets, signed URLs for temporary outside access, lifecycle rules for age-based class changes and deletion, soft delete for recovery, and the Pricing Calculator with class minimums, retrieval fees and Autoclass in mind for cost.

days.title: Managing Databases and Data Jobs: Queries, Backups, Job Status, Database Center and CMEK

concepts.heading: Running Queries Against Each Database
concepts.body: Each database has its own tool. For Cloud SQL, gcloud sql connect INSTANCE --user=root opens the mysql or psql client from Cloud Shell and allowlists the Cloud Shell address for 5 minutes, so you never add 0.0.0.0/0 to authorized networks. AlloyDB Studio is a SQL editor in the console. For BigQuery, bq query --use_legacy_sql=false runs GoogleSQL; --dry_run returns the bytes the query would process without running it, and LIMIT does not reduce the bytes scanned. Spanner takes SQL from gcloud spanner databases execute-sql DB --instance=INST --sql="SELECT ...". Bigtable uses the cbt tool: cbt read TABLE prefix=pump-17# count=20 for a prefix scan, cbt lookup for one row key, cbt count for a row count. Firestore queries come from the console or client libraries, and each is served by an index: single-field indexes are automatic, while a query combining several fields needs a composite index you create.

concepts.heading: Cloud SQL Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery
concepts.body: Cloud SQL takes automated daily backups when enabled, plus on-demand backups before a risky change. A backup can be restored to the same instance, or to a new or existing instance in the same or another project or region; restoring onto an existing instance overwrites its data. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) answers the classic incident: an UPDATE without a WHERE clause ran at 14:05 and you want the data as of 14:04. PITR needs automated backups and, for MySQL, binary logging already on before the mistake; turning them on afterwards cannot go back. PITR always creates a new instance, for example with gcloud sql instances clone SOURCE TARGET --point-in-time=TIMESTAMP, with its own name and address; you then copy the damaged tables back or repoint the application. Read replicas are not backups: a bad UPDATE replicates to them within seconds.

concepts.heading: Backups in Spanner, AlloyDB, Bigtable and Firestore
concepts.body: The other databases share one pattern: a restore creates something new instead of overwriting what is live. Spanner takes full backups on demand, or full and incremental backups through a backup schedule, and keeps them up to one year. A backup lives in the same instance, region and project as its database and can be copied to an instance in another region or project. A Spanner restore always writes a new database; you cannot restore over an existing one. A default backup schedule covers only new databases in an instance, never existing ones. AlloyDB restores backups, and point-in-time recovery from continuous backup, into a new cluster. Bigtable restores a backup to a new table. Firestore restores a backup to a new database, and a Firestore PITR clone is also a new database. So a restore never repairs just the damaged table in place: restore beside production and move the data you need.

concepts.heading: Checking the Status of BigQuery and Dataflow Jobs
concepts.body: Loads, queries, exports and copies in BigQuery run as jobs. bq ls -j -a (--jobs=true --all=true) lists recent jobs from all users, which matters because a nightly load usually runs as a service account. bq show --job=true --format=prettyjson JOB_ID shows a job's state and error details, and bq cancel JOB_ID stops a running job; it never retries a failed one. Job history in BigQuery Studio shows the same in the console. For Dataflow, gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active shows running jobs, gcloud dataflow jobs describe JOB_ID shows one, and the console draws the pipeline graph with per-step metrics. To stop a streaming job without losing in-flight data, drain it with gcloud dataflow jobs drain: it stops reading input and finishes buffered work. Cancel stops at once and can lose buffered data; force cancel is only for a job stuck while cancelling.

concepts.heading: Database Center and Customer-Managed Encryption Keys
concepts.body: Database Center is an AI-assisted dashboard with one view of a database fleet across projects: health issues such as missing backups, availability configuration, security and compliance for Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore, Memorystore and more, with recommendations and a Gemini chat. Its data is not real time and can lag up to 24 hours. Per-instance query performance is a different tool (day 18). Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) put the Cloud KMS key under the company's control. Two steps always apply: create the key in the same location as the resource, and grant the product's service agent, not users, CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter on the key. A Cloud Storage bucket can take a default CMEK at any time. Cloud SQL is stricter: CMEK is set when the instance is created and clones inherit the source's key, so an existing instance moves to CMEK by creating a new CMEK instance and migrating the data. If the Cloud SQL service agent loses key access, the instance is suspended.

examPoints: A question that names one database and asks for the command to run a query or a scan is testing the matching tool: gcloud sql connect, bq query, gcloud spanner databases execute-sql, cbt read or AlloyDB Studio, never one product's tool on another.

A question about undoing a bad write is testing that Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery needs backups and binary logging already on, and that restores in Cloud SQL PITR, Spanner, AlloyDB, Bigtable and Firestore create a new resource beside production.
A question with CMEK in the stem is testing the key location, the service agent's Encrypter/Decrypter role, and for Cloud SQL that the key is chosen only when the instance is created.

quiz.q: Compliance now requires that an existing Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance, created with Google default encryption, use a Cloud KMS key the company controls. What should the engineer do?
choices: Edit the existing instance and select the Cloud KMS key, which re-encrypts its disks during the next maintenance window
Grant the Cloud SQL service agent the CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role, which switches the existing instance to the key
Create a new instance with the key chosen at creation, after granting its service agent access, then migrate the data to it
Turn on point-in-time recovery, then clone the instance, because a clone can be given a different key from its source
quiz.explain: Cloud SQL sets CMEK when an instance is created and clones inherit the source's key, so the data must move to a new CMEK instance whose service agent can use the key. Choice B is tempting because that grant is a required step, but on its own it never changes the encryption of an existing instance.

quiz.q: A developer dropped a table in the Spanner database inventory at 10:00. A full on-demand backup was taken at 02:00, and the rest of the database must keep its writes from this morning. What should the team do?
choices: Restore the backup into a new database, then copy the dropped table back from it or repoint the application to it
Restore the backup over the existing database, which brings back only the dropped table and keeps today's writes
Run gcloud sql backups restore against the Spanner instance, which rewinds the database to the backup's version time
Ask Database Center to roll back the change, because it records schema changes and can undo them for each database
quiz.explain: A Spanner restore always creates a new database, so the team restores beside production and copies the table back. Choice B is tempting because it sounds like the least work, but Spanner never restores over a live database, and no restore brings back a single table on its own.

days.recap: Query each database with its own tool, remember that Cloud SQL PITR needs backups and binary logging and creates a new instance, expect Spanner, AlloyDB, Bigtable and Firestore restores to create new resources, drain streaming Dataflow jobs, use Database Center for fleet health, and set CMEK with a same-location key and the service agent's Encrypter/Decrypter role.

days.title: Managing Networks: Subnets, Static IPs, Routes, Cloud DNS, Cloud NAT and Firewalls

concepts.heading: Expanding Subnets and Reserving Static IP Addresses
concepts.body: When a subnet runs out of addresses, gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range SUBNET --region=REGION --prefix-length=22 widens its primary range, for example from /24 to /22, without interrupting traffic. It is one way: a primary range can never be shrunk, and the new range must not overlap another subnet. Firewall rules and routes that list the old CIDR do not grow with it. Ephemeral external addresses are released when the VM stops or is deleted. To keep the exact address a VM uses, for instance one a partner allowlisted, promote it to static with gcloud compute addresses create NAME --addresses=IP --region=REGION; reserving a new address gives a different one. Internal addresses work the same way: promote 10.10.4.17 before deleting the VM, then name it when creating the replacement. External static addresses are regional for VMs and regional load balancers, and global for global external Application Load Balancers.

concepts.heading: Custom Static Routes
concepts.body: Every VPC network has system routes: a subnet route per subnet range and a default route for 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway at priority 1000. gcloud compute routes create adds a custom static route with a destination range, a next hop, and optionally a priority and network tags. The most specific destination wins first; among equal destinations the lower priority number wins, so a route at 900 beats the default at 1000. Network tags limit a route to tagged VMs, which is how only tagged VMs go through an inspection appliance while the rest keep the default route. Next hops include an instance, an internal IP address, an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer for highly available appliances, a Cloud VPN tunnel or the default internet gateway. A VM that forwards others' packets needs --can-ip-forward at creation, or it drops traffic not addressed to it. Routes only choose a path; allowing or denying traffic is the firewall's job.

concepts.heading: Cloud DNS Zones and Cloud NAT
concepts.body: Cloud DNS hosts managed zones. A public zone answers the internet only after the registrar points the domain to the zone's Cloud DNS name servers; skipping that is the usual reason a new record never resolves. A private zone answers only inside its authorized VPC networks, so when a second network gets NXDOMAIN, add it with gcloud dns managed-zones update ZONE --networks=vpc-a,vpc-b, keeping the existing networks in the list. Custom names for VMs belong in a private zone, not in Compute Engine internal DNS. Cloud NAT gives VMs without external addresses outbound internet access with no unsolicited inbound connections. A Public NAT gateway belongs to one region and one Cloud Router there, so VMs in two regions need two gateways. Automatic NAT IP allocation adds or removes addresses as needed; when a partner allowlists fixed source addresses, reserve static external addresses and assign them manually. Choose which subnets each gateway serves, and enable NAT logging to see translations and errors.

concepts.heading: VPC Firewall Rules: Priority, Updates and Disabling
concepts.body: A VPC firewall rule has a direction, a priority from 0 to 65535, an action, targets (all instances, network tags or a service account), sources or destinations, and protocols. The matching rule with the lowest priority number decides, however specific other rules are; at equal priority a deny beats an allow. Every network has two implied rules at 65535, deny all ingress and allow all egress; they cannot be edited or deleted, but higher-priority rules override them. A rule's name, network, action and direction cannot be changed, so to turn an allow into a deny you create a new rule and delete the old one; priority, targets, ranges and ports can be updated. To test without a rule, run gcloud compute firewall-rules update RULE --disabled: it keeps its settings but is not enforced, and --no-disabled enforces it again. Removing all target tags does not switch a rule off: a rule with no target applies to every instance in the network.

concepts.heading: Cloud NGFW Policies and Firewall Rules Logging
concepts.body: Cloud Next Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW) also groups rules into firewall policies. Hierarchical firewall policies attach to the organization or folders and are evaluated before the VPC network's rules, so a deny there blocks traffic that a project rule at priority 0 allows; only an administrator at that level can relax it, for example by changing the action to goto_next, which passes evaluation to the next level. Global network firewall policies cover all regions of one VPC network and regional ones a single region, evaluated beside the VPC rules in a defined order. Logging is per rule: add --enable-logging when creating or updating a VPC rule, and --logging-metadata to drop metadata and save storage. Each entry records source, destination, ports and the matching rule. Implied rules and goto_next rules cannot log, so to log what the implied deny drops, add your own deny-all ingress rule at priority 65534 with logging on.

examPoints: A question about running out of subnet addresses or keeping an IP across a VM rebuild is testing expand-ip-range, which only grows a range, and promoting the address already in use to static.

A question in which an allow rule seems to be ignored is testing that the lowest priority number wins, that hierarchical policies are evaluated first, and that a rule's action and direction cannot be updated.

A question about private VMs reaching the internet from fixed addresses, or a zone that does not resolve, is testing regional Cloud NAT with manual static IPs, registrar delegation for public zones and authorized networks for private zones.

quiz.q: During an incident, an engineer wants to stop enforcing the VPC firewall rule allow-legacy-app for an hour to see whether anything breaks, and then restore it exactly as it was. What is the simplest approach?
choices: Delete the rule and recreate it later from the saved output of gcloud compute firewall-rules describe
Update the rule with --disabled, and later update it with --no-disabled to enforce it exactly as before
Raise the rule's priority number to 65535, which stops it from being evaluated until it is lowered again
Remove every target tag from the rule, which keeps the rule in the network without matching any of the VMs
quiz.explain: A disabled rule keeps all of its settings but is not enforced, and --no-disabled enforces it again. Choice D is tempting because it sounds like detaching the rule, but a rule with no target applies to every instance in the network, which widens it instead of switching it off.

quiz.q: A Public NAT gateway on a Cloud Router in us-east1 gives private VMs internet access. A new subnet in europe-west1, in the same VPC network, also has VMs without external addresses, and they cannot reach the internet. What should the engineer do?
choices: Add the europe-west1 subnet to the existing us-east1 gateway's list of subnets that it translates for
Create a custom static route for 0.0.0.0/0 in europe-west1 with the us-east1 NAT gateway as its next hop
Give the europe-west1 VMs ephemeral external addresses, which Cloud NAT then translates to its own IPs
Create a Cloud Router and a Public NAT gateway in europe-west1, because each NAT gateway serves one region
quiz.explain: Cloud NAT is regional, so the europe-west1 subnet needs its own Cloud Router and gateway in that region. Choice A is tempting because a gateway does have a subnet list, but it can only include subnets from its own region.

days.recap: Grow subnets with expand-ip-range (never shrink), promote addresses in use to static, steer selected traffic with tagged custom routes at a lower priority number, delegate public zones and authorize networks for private ones, place a Cloud NAT gateway in each region, and manage firewalls by priority, disabling, per-rule logging and hierarchical-first evaluation.

days.title: Monitoring: Alerting Policies, Custom Metrics, Ops Agent, Prometheus and Operations Tools
services: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

concepts.heading: Alerting Policies and Notification Channels
concepts.body: Cloud Monitoring, part of Google Cloud Observability, alerts through alerting policies: one or more conditions, notification channels and optional documentation such as a runbook link. A metric-threshold condition is met when a metric stays above or below a value for the whole retest window, for example CPU above 85 percent for 10 minutes, so a short spike pages nobody. A metric-absence condition is met when a time series sends no data for the retest window, at most 24 hours; it catches a dead agent or a job that stopped reporting, which a threshold condition cannot see. A forecasted metric-value condition predicts that a threshold will be crossed within the forecast window, such as a disk filling up. Channels include email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty, Pub/Sub and webhooks, and one policy can notify several. Uptime checks probe an HTTP, HTTPS or TCP endpoint from several locations; attach an alerting policy to learn when one fails.

concepts.heading: User-Defined Metrics and Log-Based Metrics
concepts.body: Built-in metrics cover infrastructure, but some values only your application knows. A value inside the program, such as an in-memory queue length, must be reported as a user-defined metric; Google recommends OpenTelemetry, and on Compute Engine the Ops Agent's OTLP receiver forwards it. It is then charted and alerted on like a built-in metric. If the information is already in logs, a log-based metric turns matching entries into a time series without code changes. A counter metric counts entries matching a filter, such as failed requests, and labels extracted from fields such as endpoint give one series per value. A distribution metric extracts a number such as latency_ms into histogram buckets for percentiles. User-defined log-based metrics are counters or distributions, and they are never retroactive: a metric created today has no data for yesterday.

concepts.heading: Ops Agent and Managed Service for Prometheus
concepts.body: A Compute Engine VM sends no guest logs or memory and disk-usage metrics until an agent runs on it. The Ops Agent is the primary, preferred agent: logs and metrics in one agent, configured in YAML. To collect a log at a custom path such as /var/log/orders/app.log, add a files receiver to the configuration and restart the agent. The VM's service account needs Logs Writer and Monitoring Metric Writer. Standard maintenance and regular bug fixes for the legacy Monitoring and Logging agents ended on 28 September 2026, starting a 12-month migration grace period, so a legacy agent is never the answer for new work. Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus keeps Prometheus and PromQL without running Prometheus servers. Managed collection is recommended: an operator handles scraping and scaling, the data lands in the same global store as Cloud Monitoring, is kept for 24 months and is queried with PromQL across clusters, and existing Grafana dashboards keep working.

concepts.heading: Finding Slow Code and Slow Queries
concepts.body: Three tools answer three performance questions. Cloud Trace follows a request across services as timed spans, so for a slow checkout you see which downstream call adds latency. Cloud Profiler continuously samples CPU and memory use of running code with low overhead and attributes it to functions. It runs inside your own processes, so it cannot be installed in a managed database. For databases, Cloud SQL query insights shows the queries that load an instance most, their latency and the application tags that issued them. Index advisor and 30-day metrics retention need Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, so downgrading to Enterprise edition removes them. A slow call between microservices points to Trace, a CPU hot spot to Profiler, and a heavy SQL statement to query insights. VPC Flow Logs and uptime checks show neither code time nor query time.

concepts.heading: Personalized Service Health, Active Assist, Cloud Hub and Gemini Cloud Assist
concepts.body: Personalized Service Health (PSH) shows Google Cloud incidents relevant to your projects through a dashboard, an API and logs in Cloud Logging, with alerts on events; the public status page is not filtered to your projects. Active Assist is the family of recommendations about cost, security, performance and manageability; for example, the idle VM recommender (gcloud recommender recommendations list --recommender=google.compute.instance.IdleResourceRecommender) finds VMs with almost no use and suggests stopping them. Cloud Hub gives one operational view of a project or an App Hub application spanning projects: health and alerts, Google Cloud incidents, quota usage and maintenance. Gemini Cloud Assist investigations do AI-assisted root-cause analysis: started from an alert, a log entry or Cloud Hub, they gather observations from logs, metrics and configuration, rank probable causes and recommend next steps, each linked to its source data.

examPoints: A question about being notified is testing the condition type: metric threshold with a retest window for high values, metric absence (window up to 24 hours) for missing data, plus one notification channel per destination.

A question about a value that is never logged, or one that already appears in logs, is testing user-defined metrics with OpenTelemetry versus counter or distribution log-based metrics, which are never backfilled.

A question that lists Trace, Profiler, query insights, PSH, Active Assist, Cloud Hub and Gemini Cloud Assist is testing which single question each tool answers, and that the Ops Agent replaces the legacy agents.

quiz.q: A batch export job on a VM runs every two hours and writes a custom metric each time it finishes. The team wants an alert if the job silently stops, so that no data point arrives for three hours. Which condition should the alerting policy use?
choices: A metric-threshold condition on the job's metric that is met when its value is above zero for a three-hour retest window
An uptime check against the VM's external address, which fails as soon as the job stops writing its custom metric
A log-based counter metric created today, which backfills the job's earlier entries to find the runs that it missed
A metric-absence condition on the job's metric that is met when the time series sends no data for three hours
quiz.explain: A metric-absence condition is met when a time series sends no data for the retest window (at most 24 hours), which is exactly a job that stopped. Choice A is tempting because thresholds are the usual alert, but a threshold condition compares data points that arrive, and a stopped job sends none.

quiz.q: A team still runs the legacy Monitoring and Logging agents on its Compute Engine VMs, and the platform lead asks what to do now that their standard maintenance has ended. What should the engineer recommend?
choices: Keep the legacy agents, because Google still releases regular bug fixes and support for new operating systems
Migrate the VMs to the Ops Agent, which collects both logs and metrics and is the preferred Compute Engine agent
Install Cloud Profiler on each VM, which now collects the system metrics and logs that the legacy agents sent
Delete the agents without a replacement, because Cloud Monitoring now reads guest memory and logs by itself
quiz.explain: Standard maintenance for the legacy agents ended on 28 September 2026, and the Ops Agent is the preferred replacement for logs and metrics. Choice D is tempting because some VM metrics need no agent, but guest logs and metrics such as memory use still need one.

days.recap: Alert with threshold, absence or forecast conditions and notification channels, report in-code values as user-defined metrics and logged values as counter or distribution log-based metrics, run the Ops Agent instead of the legacy agents, keep PromQL with Managed Service for Prometheus, and match Trace, Profiler, query insights, PSH, Active Assist, Cloud Hub and Gemini Cloud Assist to their questions.

days.title: Logging: Audit Logs, VPC Flow Logs, Firewall Logs, Log Router, Log Buckets and Queries

concepts.heading: Cloud Audit Logs: Admin Activity, Data Access and More
concepts.body: Cloud Audit Logs answer who did what, where and when through Google Cloud APIs. Admin Activity audit logs record calls that change configuration or metadata, such as creating a VM or changing an allow policy; they are always written and cannot be configured, excluded or disabled. System Event audit logs record actions by Google systems, such as autoscaling adding VMs to a managed instance group, and are also always written. Data Access audit logs record reads of configuration or metadata and reads or writes of user data, as ADMIN_READ, DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE. Being large, they are disabled by default except for BigQuery: if an auditor asks who downloaded bucket objects last week and nobody enabled DATA_READ for Cloud Storage, those entries never existed; enable them now for the future. Policy Denied audit logs record requests refused by a security policy such as VPC Service Controls. Reading Data Access logs needs Private Logs Viewer (roles/logging.privateLogViewer); Logs Viewer sees the other types.

concepts.heading: VPC Flow Logs and Firewall Rules Logging
concepts.body: VPC Flow Logs samples packets of VMs, GKE nodes and other resources and aggregates them per connection and interval. Enable it per subnet or more widely, and cut volume by lengthening the aggregation interval from the default 5 seconds up to 15 minutes, lowering the secondary sampling rate, filtering or dropping metadata; Google controls the primary sampling rate. Flow logs also write separate records for dropped traffic, with disposition=DROPPED and a drop_reason such as FIREWALL_DENY, aggregated per flow and reason with estimated packet counts, not one record per rejected attempt. Firewall Rules Logging works per rule: every connection matching a rule with logging enabled is recorded with source, destination, ports and the rule's name, which proves which rule allowed or denied it. Implied rules cannot log, so a logged deny-all rule at 65534 captures what the implied deny would drop. Neither appears in audit logs, because connections are not API calls.

concepts.heading: Log Router, Sinks and Exclusions
concepts.body: In the Log Router, sinks decide where each entry goes. Each project starts with two sinks: _Required sends Admin Activity, System Event and Access Transparency logs to the _Required bucket and cannot be changed; _Default sends everything else to the _Default bucket and can be edited. A sink has one inclusion filter and any number of exclusion filters; an entry is routed when it matches the inclusion filter and no exclusion. To stop storing noise such as health-check probes, add an exclusion to the _Default sink. Destinations are a log bucket, a BigQuery dataset, a Cloud Storage bucket for archives, Pub/Sub for streaming to outside tools such as a SIEM, or another project. A sink writes through its writer identity, a service account that needs a role on the destination, such as BigQuery Data Editor on a dataset. An aggregated sink on an organization or folder with --include-children routes logs from every current and future child project.

concepts.heading: Log Buckets and Retention
concepts.body: Log buckets store entries in Cloud Logging. The _Required bucket keeps logs for 400 days, which cannot be changed. The _Default bucket keeps them 30 days by default, adjustable from 1 to 3650 days, for example with gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=90. User-defined buckets, such as one with 365-day retention in a security project, receive chosen logs through a sink. Buckets have a location, which matters for data residency, and IAM, including log views that expose part of a bucket, controls access. Raising retention keeps logs searchable in Logs Explorer for longer; exporting to Cloud Storage keeps them outside Logs Explorer. A sink routes only new entries, so a sink created today does not move last month's logs. For central collection, combine an aggregated sink with a user-defined bucket in one project.

concepts.heading: Filtering Logs and Observability Analytics
concepts.body: Logs Explorer uses the Logging query language. Comparisons join with uppercase AND, OR and NOT; severity>=ERROR returns ERROR, CRITICAL, ALERT and EMERGENCY, while severity="ERROR" returns one level. The colon is the has operator: textPayload:"timeout" matches the word anywhere, textPayload="timeout" only an entry whose whole text is that word, and =~ takes a regular expression. Common fields are resource.type (gce_instance, k8s_container), logName (for example containing cloudaudit.googleapis.com) and protoPayload.methodName for audit entries. Logs Explorer finds entries and its histogram counts them, but it cannot compute averages or groups. For that, upgrade a log bucket to use Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics) and run SQL with GROUP BY, AVG and joins over the logs in place. A linked BigQuery dataset is read only and lets BigQuery query the same data, but it must never be a sink destination.

examPoints: A question asking who changed something or who read data is testing Admin Activity logs, which are always on, versus Data Access logs, which must be enabled per service except BigQuery and need Private Logs Viewer to read.

A question about where logs should go is testing sink destinations: Pub/Sub for streaming to outside tools, Cloud Storage for archives, BigQuery or log buckets for analysis, plus the writer identity's role and aggregated sinks for whole organizations.

A question about blocked or dropped traffic is testing that firewall rules logging records each matching connection per rule, while VPC Flow Logs gives aggregated DROPPED records with estimated counts.

quiz.q: Firewall Rules Logging is enabled on several VPC rules in a project, and the entries land in the _Default bucket. Security wants only those firewall entries kept for 365 days, while other logs keep the current 30 days. What should the engineer configure?
choices: A user-defined log bucket with 365-day retention, and a sink whose inclusion filter matches the firewall log entries
A 365-day retention on the _Required bucket, because firewall logs are stored in it together with the audit logs
A counter log-based metric on the firewall entries, because a log-based metric keeps each matching entry for a year
Data Access audit logs for the Compute Engine API, which keep each firewall decision in the project for 400 days
quiz.explain: A user-defined bucket with its own retention, fed by a sink matching only the firewall entries, keeps them a year without changing other logs. Choice B is tempting because _Required keeps logs 400 days, but it holds only audit-type logs and its retention cannot be changed.

quiz.q: A network engineer has VPC Flow Logs enabled on a subnet and wants to know how much traffic to its VMs is being blocked by firewall rules. Which statement about what flow logs can show is correct?
choices: Flow logs never include blocked traffic, so only firewall rules logging can show that a packet was denied
Flow logs record every denied connection attempt exactly once, so they fully replace logging on deny rules
Flow logs can write separate records marked DROPPED with a drop reason and estimated packet counts
Flow logs show blocked traffic only after Data Access audit logs are enabled for the Compute Engine API
quiz.explain: VPC Flow Logs writes records with disposition DROPPED and a drop reason such as a firewall deny, aggregated with estimated counts, so they estimate the blocked traffic. Choice A is tempting because firewall rules logging is the classic answer, but it gives per-rule evidence and is not the only source of dropped-traffic data.

days.recap: Admin Activity and System Event logs are always on and kept 400 days in _Required, Data Access logs are opt-in except for BigQuery, sinks route entries by inclusion and exclusion filters to buckets, BigQuery, Cloud Storage or Pub/Sub, retention is set per bucket, and Observability Analytics adds SQL over logs in place.

days.title: IAM: Allow Policies, Role Types, Custom Roles, Conditions, Deny Policies and Troubleshooting

concepts.heading: Allow Policies, Bindings and Inheritance
concepts.body: Access is granted through an allow policy on a resource: the organization, a folder, a project or a resource such as a bucket or a Pub/Sub topic. Each resource has one allow policy, made of role bindings that tie one role to principals such as user:, group:, serviceAccount: or domain:, optionally with a condition. Read it with gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT, add a binding with gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT --member=group:ops@example.com --role=roles/compute.viewer, and remove one with remove-iam-policy-binding. A script using set-iam-policy must read, modify, write: the etag detects a concurrent change, and a 409 conflict means read again and reapply. Policies are inherited downward, so effective access is the union of a resource's policy and every ancestor's. A folder grant reaches every project below it, and removing a direct project grant changes nothing while the folder grant remains; a lower level can never cancel an inherited grant.

concepts.heading: Basic, Legacy Basic, Predefined and Custom Roles
concepts.body: Basic roles are broad roles with thousands of permissions across services. The current basic roles are Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer) and Reader (roles/reader); they are granted only with gcloud or the API, not the console, and accept IAM Conditions. Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor) and Viewer (roles/viewer) are now legacy basic roles and cannot be used in conditional bindings. Google says not to grant either set in production unless there is no alternative. Predefined roles are maintained by Google for one service and job, such as Pub/Sub Publisher, BigQuery Data Viewer or Compute Instance Admin (v1), and gain permissions as services add features. Custom roles are permission lists you define when no predefined role is narrow enough. Least privilege means the narrowest role on the smallest resource: Publisher on one topic rather than Editor on the project, or BigQuery Data Viewer on a dataset plus BigQuery Job User on the project for an analyst who runs queries.

concepts.heading: Custom Roles: Levels, Launch Stages and Lifecycle
concepts.body: A custom role is created in an organization or a project, never a folder, and can be granted only inside it: an organization role on any folder, project or resource in that organization, a project role only in its project. Creating one needs Role Administrator (roles/iam.roleAdmin) for project roles or Organization Role Administrator (roles/iam.organizationRoleAdmin) for organization roles; Project IAM Admin can grant roles but not create them. To trim a predefined role, copy it with gcloud iam roles copy and remove permissions; gcloud iam list-testable-permissions shows which permissions a custom role may contain. Custom roles never receive the permissions Google later adds to the role they were copied from. Launch stages such as ALPHA, BETA, GA and DEPRECATED are informational; DISABLED keeps the role in policies but grants nothing, and is reversible. A deleted role can be undeleted within 7 days, its bindings inert meanwhile, and its ID is reusable only after permanent deletion, up to 44 days later.

concepts.heading: IAM Conditions and Deny Policies
concepts.body: IAM Conditions make a binding apply only when a Common Expression Language expression is true, for temporary access such as request.time < timestamp("2027-01-01T00:00:00Z") or resource-based access such as resource.name.startsWith(...) with a resource.type check so other resource types in the role are not blocked. Conditional bindings need policy version 3 and cannot use legacy basic roles. A condition never narrows access that an unconditional binding of the same role already gives. Deny policies work the other way: denied principals, optional exception principals and denied permissions in v2 format, such as compute.googleapis.com/instances.delete. They attach only to an organization, folder or project, are inherited below, and are checked before allow policies, so no role, Owner included, overrides them. Deny conditions recognize only resource tags. Managing deny policies needs Deny Admin (roles/iam.denyAdmin), which Owner does not include. The pattern: grant high in the hierarchy, deny the one exception.

concepts.heading: Recommender, Policy Troubleshooter and Admin Roles
concepts.body: IAM role recommendations, part of Active Assist, compare each principal's granted permissions with those it actually used and suggest removing a role or replacing it with a smaller one, the evidence-based way to trim old Editor grants. Policy Troubleshooter takes a principal, a resource and a permission and explains which binding grants access and which deny rule blocks it: the answer to why someone cannot do something. Security Reviewer (roles/iam.securityReviewer) lists resources and reads their allow policies without changing anything, which suits an auditor on the organization. Project IAM Admin (roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin) manages a project's allow policy without permissions to create VMs, buckets or databases; Folder IAM Admin does the same for a folder. Because a policy admin can grant themselves more, conditions can limit which roles they may grant.

examPoints: A question in which removing a grant does not remove access is testing inheritance: allow policies are a union down the hierarchy, and only the higher grant or a deny policy takes the access away.

A question about conditions failing or roles being too broad is testing that legacy basic roles take no conditions, that basic roles are discouraged, and that predefined roles at the smallest resource are preferred.
