A question about custom roles is testing organization or project level only, Role Administrator (project) or Organization Role Administrator to create them, DISABLED as the only stage that changes access, and that copies never pick up new permissions.

quiz.q: An engineer runs gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding with --role=roles/editor and a condition that ends access on 31 December for a contractor group. The command fails. What is the reason, and what should the engineer do?
choices: Conditions need policy version 1, so the engineer should add --policy-version=1 and rerun the same command
Conditions work only on folder bindings, so the engineer should grant Editor with the condition on the folder
Legacy basic roles take no conditions, so the engineer should grant the needed predefined roles with it
Conditions cannot test request.time, so the engineer should use a resource.name check with the same role
quiz.explain: Owner, Editor and Viewer are legacy basic roles that cannot be used in conditional bindings, while predefined roles accept the condition and follow least privilege. Choice A is tempting because policy version matters, but conditions need version 3, and no version lifts the role restriction.

quiz.q: A new engineer reads that Google Cloud has changed its basic roles. Which role IDs are the current basic roles, as opposed to the legacy basic roles?
choices: roles/owner, roles/editor and roles/viewer, which are the only basic roles that accept IAM Conditions
roles/admin, roles/contributor and roles/reader, which are granted on the IAM page of the console
roles/owner, roles/writer and roles/viewer, which mix the legacy role names with the current ones
roles/admin, roles/writer and roles/reader, which are granted with the gcloud CLI or the IAM API
quiz.explain: Admin, Writer and Reader are the current basic roles, granted with gcloud or the API. Choice A is tempting because those names are familiar, but Owner, Editor and Viewer are the legacy set, precisely the roles that cannot take conditions.

days.recap: Allow policies are unions inherited down the hierarchy; Admin, Writer and Reader are the current basic roles and Owner, Editor and Viewer the legacy ones; predefined roles on the smallest resource give least privilege; custom roles live in organizations or projects; conditions and deny policies refine access; recommender and Policy Troubleshooter right-size and explain it.

days.title: Service Accounts: Creating, Attaching, Impersonation and Workload Identity Federation

concepts.heading: Creating Service Accounts and Recognizing the Three Kinds
concepts.body: gcloud iam service-accounts create etl-runner --display-name="ETL runner" gives etl-runner@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com; the ID cannot be changed later. A new account can take 60 seconds or more to be usable, so scripts retry with exponential backoff. User-managed service accounts are ones you create. Default service accounts are user-managed accounts that some services create when enabled, such as the Compute Engine default PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com. Service agents, such as service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com, are Google-managed accounts a service uses to act on your resources; keep their service agent roles. Default accounts may get Editor automatically; enforce iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts to stop that, and replace Editor on existing ones yourself.

concepts.heading: Attaching Service Accounts and Roles on a Service Account
concepts.body: Workloads should use an attached account, not a key: attach one when creating a VM with --service-account=EMAIL --scopes=cloud-platform, or set the identity of a Cloud Run service or GKE node pool. Use one dedicated, minimally privileged account per application, so audit logs show which application acted. On VMs, access scopes are a legacy limit on top of IAM: the default scopes make Cloud Storage read only, so Google recommends the cloud-platform scope with IAM roles, and scopes change only while the VM is stopped. A service account is also a resource with an allow policy. Attaching it needs iam.serviceAccounts.actAs, in Service Account User (roles/iam.serviceAccountUser). Grant it on the single account, not the project, which would cover every service account there. Attaching an account from another project needs iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage not enforced on the account's project.

concepts.heading: Impersonation and Short-Lived Credentials Instead of Keys
concepts.body: Impersonation means acting as a service account with short-lived credentials. The caller needs Service Account Token Creator (roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator) on the target account, which includes getAccessToken; Service Account OpenID Connect Identity Token Creator covers only ID tokens. For one command, add --impersonate-service-account=EMAIL; for a session, set the auth/impersonate_service_account property. For local code, gcloud auth application-default login --impersonate-service-account=EMAIL gives client libraries the account's tokens through Application Default Credentials. Access tokens last 1 hour, or up to 12 hours if the iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension constraint lists the account. Keys are the risky alternative: a key works from anywhere and does not expire unless an expiry policy is set; avoid them and enforce iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation. The pair: attach means Service Account User, impersonate means Token Creator.

concepts.heading: Workload Identity Federation for GKE
concepts.body: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Pods call Google Cloud APIs as their Kubernetes service account (KSA), not the node's account or a key. Autopilot always has it on. On Standard, enable it with --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog and update existing node pools with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA so Pods use the GKE metadata server. The preferred grant is directly to the KSA as a principal on the specific resource: principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/KSA, for example Storage Object Viewer on one bucket; principalSet:// covers groups such as every KSA in a namespace. The older method grants Workload Identity User on an IAM service account to serviceAccount:PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA] and annotates the KSA with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account, for products that need a service account. All clusters in a project share one pool, so the same namespace and KSA name are one identity; keep untrusted clusters in separate projects.

concepts.heading: Workload Identity Federation for External Workloads and Retiring Accounts
concepts.body: Outside workloads, such as GitHub Actions, AWS or on-premises jobs, use Workload Identity Federation instead of keys: a workload identity pool, a provider trusting the external identity provider (for example GitHub's OIDC issuer or AWS), and an attribute condition so only tokens from your own organization or repository are accepted. The workload exchanges its token for short-lived Google credentials, for direct resource access or to impersonate a service account. A credential configuration file tells the client library where to get the external credential and which pool, provider and account to use; it holds no secrets. Workforce Identity Federation is the counterpart for human users. To retire accounts, find unused ones with service account insights and Activity Analyzer, then disable (reversible) before deleting. A deleted account can be undeleted within 30 days; recreating one with the same name gives a new identity the old bindings do not cover.

examPoints: A question with an actAs or getAccessToken error is testing the pair: Service Account User to attach an account, Token Creator to impersonate it, both granted on the single account.
A question offering a key file as a shortcut is testing keyless options: attached accounts, impersonation, Workload Identity Federation and the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint.

A question about Pods or outside workloads calling Google Cloud APIs is testing Workload Identity Federation for GKE with direct principal:// grants, or a pool, provider and attribute condition for external identities.

quiz.q: An engineer must run one gcloud command as the service account deploy-sa to test its permissions, without creating any long-lived credential. She has no roles on deploy-sa yet. What is the correct approach?
choices: Create a JSON key for deploy-sa, activate it with gcloud auth activate-service-account, then delete the key
Get Token Creator on deploy-sa, then run the command with --impersonate-service-account set to its email
Get Service Account User on deploy-sa, which makes every gcloud command she runs use that account's identity
Set the core/account property to the deploy-sa email, which switches gcloud to that account for one command
quiz.explain: Impersonation with Token Creator on the one account gives short-lived tokens for that command, with no key. Choice C is tempting because Service Account User is also a role on the account, but its actAs permission attaches the account to resources and cannot create tokens.

quiz.q: After a new API is enabled, the IAM page shows service-123456789012@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com holding a role in the project. The security lead wants it removed as unknown. How should the engineer respond?
choices: It is a Google-managed service agent that Pub/Sub uses to act in the project, and removing its role can break the service
It is a user-managed account that a teammate created, and it can be deleted because gcp-sa accounts are never needed
It is the Compute Engine default service account, so it should be disabled and replaced with a dedicated account on VMs
It is an identity created from a leaked key, so its keys should be rotated and the account removed from the project
quiz.explain: A gcp-sa address is a service agent that Google manages so the service can work with your resources, and its role should stay. Choice C is tempting because default accounts are a known risk, but the Compute Engine default account is PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com.

days.recap: Use one dedicated service account per application, know user-managed, default and service agent accounts, attach with Service Account User and impersonate with Token Creator on the single account, prefer short-lived tokens to keys, use Workload Identity Federation with principal:// grants on GKE and a pool and provider elsewhere, and disable before deleting.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, Commonly Confused Pairs, and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: The Associate Cloud Engineer exam lasts 2 hours and has 50 to 60 multiple choice and multiple select questions, so plan on roughly two minutes per question and check at the one-hour mark that you are about halfway. Google does not publish a pass mark: you receive a pass or fail result, so aim to be comfortable well above any guessed threshold rather than scraping by. The exam guide weights the four sections at about 20 percent for setting up a cloud solution environment, 30 percent for planning and implementing a cloud solution, 30 percent for ensuring successful operation and 20 percent for configuring access and security. There are no prerequisites, and Google recommends at least six months of hands-on experience. You can take the exam online with a remote proctor or at a testing center, and the certification is valid for 3 years. The exam page notes that it was updated for recent branding changes, so study current names such as Cloud Run functions, Cloud NGFW, Observability Analytics and the Admin, Writer and Reader basic roles.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Setup, Planning and Storage
concepts.body: Spanner scales writes horizontally with strong consistency across regions, while Cloud SQL and AlloyDB scale reads with replicas or read pools but send every write to one primary. Cloud Storage soft delete restores deleted objects for its retention period even with versioning off, while Object Versioning keeps overwritten and deleted generations only from the moment it is enabled. Lifecycle rules change classes or delete objects on conditions you write, while Autoclass moves objects between classes based on access. Cloud Storage has five classes: Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive work in any location type, while Rapid exists only in zonal buckets. Container Registry has shut down and Cloud Deployment Manager has reached end of support, so the answers are Artifact Registry and Infrastructure Manager or Terraform. A restore in Spanner, AlloyDB, Bigtable or Firestore, and Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery, each create a new resource. Draining a streaming Dataflow job finishes buffered work, while cancel stops at once. When a pair still feels shaky, return to its day in this plan and redo that domain's practice questions.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Operations, Networking and Security
concepts.body: In firewalls, the lowest priority number wins, deny beats allow only at equal priority, and hierarchical policies are evaluated before VPC rules; routes choose a path and never allow traffic. A metric-threshold condition needs data, while a metric-absence condition fires when data stops. Counter log-based metrics count entries and distribution metrics extract numbers, and neither is backfilled. Admin Activity audit logs are always on, while Data Access logs must be enabled except for BigQuery. Firewall rules logging records each matching connection, while VPC Flow Logs samples traffic. An exclusion filter stops storing entries, a sink routes them, and a bucket's retention decides how long they stay. Cloud Trace finds slow calls between services, Cloud Profiler finds hot code, and query insights finds heavy SQL. In IAM, Owner, Editor and Viewer are legacy basic roles and take no conditions, while Admin, Writer and Reader are the current ones. Service Account User attaches an account, Token Creator impersonates it. Custom roles live at organization or project level, never on folders.

concepts.heading: Use an Error Log
concepts.body: In the last days, more questions help less than understanding the ones you missed. Keep a simple error log with three columns: the question's topic, the rule you did not know, and the clue in the stem you should have noticed. For example: topic Cloud NAT, rule each gateway serves one region, clue "a new subnet in europe-west1". After every practice set, add new rows and reread the whole log, and redo missed questions a day later without looking at the answer. Group entries by section to see which days of this plan to revisit: days 16 to 19 cover operations and days 20 and 21 cover access and security. If one section fills half the log, spend the next session on it. Use the question bank's section filter and the mock exam with the one section only option to drill a weak area, and stop adding new material the evening before the exam. Hands-on practice in a sandbox project, running the gcloud, bq and kubectl commands from your log, fixes command questions better than rereading.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan
concepts.body: The day before, run a short timed mock, reread your error log and sleep. On the day, check your ID and your testing setup early; for an online proctored exam, clear the desk and test the system ahead of time. During the exam, read the last sentence of each scenario first so you know what is being asked, then look for the deciding clue: a region, least privilege, without downtime, no keys, minimum operational effort or a fixed source address. For multiple select questions, read the stem carefully for how many answers it wants before choosing. Eliminate answers that rely on retired or legacy features, such as Container Registry, Deployment Manager, legacy monitoring agents, service account keys or broad basic roles. If a question takes too long, choose your best answer, mark it for review and move on, and answer every item, because a blank never scores. If you do not pass, use the result to decide which sections to study again, and check Google's certification retake policy before you book another attempt.

examPoints: A question that offers a broad basic role, a key file or a retired product beside a narrower option is testing whether you choose the least-privileged, keyless and current answer.

A question with a single deciding clue, such as one region, a fixed source address, no data arriving or a read by a user, is testing whether you read for that clue before choosing among look-alike services.
A question that pairs two similar tools, such as sinks and exclusions, Trace and Profiler, or Service Account User and Token Creator, is testing which one answers the exact need in the stem.

quiz.q: An investigation needs two facts: who deleted the VM web-3 last Tuesday, and who downloaded objects from the bucket contracts-prod yesterday. Which logs answer these, assuming the required settings were in place beforehand?
choices: Data Access audit logs for the VM deletion, and Admin Activity audit logs for the object downloads
System Event audit logs for the VM deletion, and VPC Flow Logs on the subnet for the object downloads
Admin Activity audit logs for the VM deletion, and firewall rules logging for the object downloads
Admin Activity audit logs for the VM deletion, and Data Access audit logs enabled for Cloud Storage
quiz.explain: Deleting a VM changes configuration, which Admin Activity logs always record, and reading objects is a data read that Data Access logs record once enabled for Cloud Storage. Choice A is tempting because both are audit logs, but it swaps them: Data Access covers reads, Admin Activity covers changes.

quiz.q: Ana deploys a Cloud Run service that runs as app-sa. Ben needs to run gcloud commands as app-sa through impersonation to test its access. Which roles should each person receive on app-sa itself?
choices: Service Account Token Creator for Ana, and Service Account User for Ben
Service Account Admin for Ana, and Workload Identity User for Ben
Service Account User for Ana, and Service Account Token Creator for Ben
Service Account Key Admin for both, so each person can create a key file
quiz.explain: Deploying a service that runs as an account needs actAs from Service Account User, and impersonating it needs Token Creator. Choice A is tempting because it names the right two roles, but it gives them to the wrong people.

days.recap: Associate Cloud Engineer is 2 hours with 50 to 60 multiple choice and multiple select questions and an unpublished pass mark; drill the confused pairs, keep an error log, read each scenario for its deciding clue, prefer least privilege, keyless and current services, and check the retake policy before booking again.
